#9518. What Chimps Can Teach Us About Male Friendships

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Across the Western world, young men and boys face a changing economy, with fewer manual labor jobs and factory floors that used to give a swathe of working-class men purpose and value. This leaves a large portion of recent generations feeling left behind and forgotten—and vulnerable to exploitation.

A profitable industry of influencers who misframe evolutionary science to justify their narratives have taken advantage of the addictive nature of social media to hook into this vacuum and light up phone screens every night with the same vitriolic messages: “Reclaim your manhood”; “You are being feminized”; “The world is making you soft.”

But this narrative conflicts with the biological reality. Across species—from fungal networks trading nutrients underground to astronauts sharing the role of emptying the latrine on the International Space Station—every organism must strike some balance between competing and cooperating. Lessons from the animal kingdom, from my research and others, show that cooperation doesn’t diminish masculinity.

Indeed, dominant primates use their power judiciously, and male friendship forms the foundation of cooperation in a variety of species, with affectionate touch, caring, and vulnerability playing crucial roles in male relationships. The simple picture painted for these boys is built on sand. Once we observe the reality of sex, behavior, and connection in the natural world around us, it washes away.

Human males stand to improve their relationships, benefit from a broader base of emotional and social support, and enhance their well-being with these friendship lessons from our closest cousins in the animal kingdom.

One term at the core of the manosphere is the notion of alpha males. Life coaches and politicians push this construct without understanding the true function of hierarchy in the natural world. They believe that to get ahead you must take advantage of others, and that the weak get left behind. In reality, dominant male primates care for relationships and wield their power judiciously.

It’s true that male chimpanzees form typically linear dominance relationships, where one submits to another, all the way to the top. They compete, and those competitions can spill into physical altercations. Higher-ranking males do tend to sire more offspring.

But these broad truths hide the nuance of layered cooperation, care, nurturing touch, and love among male chimps. Day after day, most of that competitive pressure never turns into a fight at all. What holds chimpanzee communities together is less the male at the top and more the alliances underneath him. Males groom each other for hours at a time. They embrace after conflicts and kiss the arms and shoulders of their allies before potential competition, to resolve any tension. Before risky boundary patrols, when they might encounter rival groups, they even hold each other’s genitals—a sign of deep trust. Data spanning nearly three decades from Gombe show that males with strong ties to the alpha sired more offspring than those without, and so did males with wider networks of close allies, whether or not they ever rose in rank at all. Those who look out for each other and contribute to a strong community end up thriving.

You can see the value of those alliances when a hierarchy is disrupted. At Taï National Park in Côte d’Ivoire, Anna Preis and her colleagues measured urinary cortisol in wild males across stable and unstable dominance periods. Stress rose in every male during the unstable stretches, regardless of rank. Aggression went the other way, rising when things were calm and the group faced less risk of destabilization. When the risk of escalation was greatest, males backed off. Stability has its own payoff; a group tearing itself apart can’t defend a territory.

Indeed, even in its origins, the term “alpha” contained more nuance than broadly understood. The term rose out of research during the mid-20th century on captive wolves who were thrown together into crowded spaces without room to escape. Such an arrangement would produce a tense, despotic dynamic in any species, including our own. Once biologists began studying wild wolf packs, it became apparent that they are, well, families. They comprise a breeding pair and their grown offspring. L. David Mech, the biologist who popularized the alpha wolf in the first place, has spent more than two decades asking people to retire the term in order to accurately reflect natural communities. Despite its inaccuracy, the idea still perpetuates on podcasts and social media.

The role of vulnerability and comfort in the natural world provides another powerful lesson for humanity. At a wildlife sanctuary in Zambia, I’ve come to know a longstanding alpha male chimpanzee named Doug over many years. One day, during my first field season observing his group, he was separated from his community for routine husbandry purposes, alongside a slightly younger rival and the rival’s paternal ally. During this separation, the rival pair ambushed him, leaving him incredibly shaken. I had known Doug as a strong leader who never broke composure, and I felt shocked to see him cowering and screaming, nothing like the composed figurehead his group had respected.

A low-ranking male, whom Doug had rarely paid attention to, approached first, offering himself in a gesture of submission. What followed drew in most of the roughly 40 other chimpanzees in the group. They embraced, touched, and kissed him; exchanged genital contact; placed their hands in his mouth; and invited him to mount them. This scale of collective reassurance directed toward a single individual is something I’ve never seen since, and is likely only sparked by moments of genuine crisis. The whole group responded to Doug’s distress with an outpouring of comfort and what to humans would appear to be love.

The main aim of this project was to study consolation: how chimpanzees, and their sister species bonobos, comfort each other after fights. But we kept noticing similar intense, friendly contacts occurring in the absence of conflicts, often in the anticipation of competition. To better understand this, we conducted a feeding task with a five-minute window before the food arrived, filming 116 apes across five groups at two sanctuaries. We found that those who exchanged more reassuring contact beforehand went on to spend significantly more time feeding peacefully alongside others. In chimpanzees, males exhibited most of this behavior, but primarily in Doug’s more tolerant group. In a more despotic group where resources were less evenly distributed, the male-male relationships were markedly weaker. Simply put, friendship and reassuring behaviors among males helped these chimps peacefully put aside competing interests, which may lay the groundwork for collective harmony.

Some of these behaviors require remarkable trust. Placing a finger, or even a whole hand, inside another male’s mouth or pressing your own mouth to someone’s body after they’ve just been attacked may be misinterpreted as having aggressive intent and could spark a new conflict. Chimpanzees have a reputation for amputating the extremities of others, and that, along with the size of their canines, makes these behaviors exceptionally risky during such turbulent times. Our hypothesis: That could be the point. You only offer that kind of vulnerability to someone you trust not to use it against you, and doing so signals something about the relationship that a show of strength can’t. Again, we noticed that these behaviors were particularly amplified in Doug’s group compared to the one with a less benevolent leader.

Doug remains alpha to this day, and from our research, his tenureship seems to be thanks to the bonds he continues to invest in and the support he shows for his peers. He’s flawed and sometimes lashes out as any male chimpanzee might do, but throughout the seven years we’ve studied him, no challenges have managed to displace him. Doug looks out for others, and in turn they look out for him. Over my time studying many groups of chimpanzees, it seems the most tolerant social environments emerge from the leadership of strong, stable, and generally fair alphas who allow others access to resources and who keep tight bonds with their closest allies.

Humans can also learn from the way male chimpanzees can be tender in other contexts. At Taï National Park in Côte d’Ivoire, researchers recorded wild chimpanzees adopting orphaned infants, more than half of them taken in by males with no obvious kinship reason to bother. One adult male, Porthos, adopted an unrelated infant female named Gia and carried her on his back for years, sharing food with her long after any potential social debt to her deceased mother had lapsed. Later analysis found that what predicted whether a male took on that role was not the infant’s sex, and not relatedness, but the strength of the grooming bond he’d shared with the mother before she died.

Touch carries power in humans, as well. Research across five European cultures found that the area of the body you’ll let someone touch maps almost directly onto the strength of your emotional bond with them. There is cultural variation. British people are notably more guarded about casual contact than many of their European neighbours, and touch between men in many Western contexts carries particular social weight. Touch conveys intimacy and trust. Yet holding someone’s hand or shoulder can also be used to intimidate or harass. We could learn from primates to stop withholding touch where it would help most and back down from reaching for it where it shouldn’t be used at all.

One key area where more touch helps is sports. A study of all 30 NBA teams during the 2008–09 season found that the teams who touched more early in the season, through fist bumps, chest bumps, hugs, and high fives, went on to perform better and play more cooperatively later, even after controlling for player salaries and pre-season expectations. In women’s college basketball, players who received more physical contact from teammates after missing their first free throw were more likely to convert the second. After five straight shootout losses, England’s governing body in football, the FA, spent 18 months rebuilding England’s approach to penalties under Gareth Southgate, not just the technical side. Players were coached on how to treat each other after a miss. They learned to place an arm around the shoulder rather than leaving each other isolated. Celebrating wildly after a scored kick became a deliberate technique for steadying whoever was up next. Locker-room culture has never been shy about physical contact between teammates. Now we know that the contact might be doing real work.

To be sure, humans show exceptional diversity in our cultures and behavior, for better and worse. But when humans are violent or cruel, people call it primal, or animalistic. We emphasize our altruism as unique to our species. That’s unfair to animals. Humans have bullied others until they took their own lives. We’ve wiped out entire tribes and cultures. And beyond targeting other people, even now, humans are removing protections for endangered keystone species that ecosystems depend upon to thrive. But we don’t need to accept the drive to dominate as inevitable. If the apes show anything, it’s how much of that drive gets managed and set aside day to day, and how much depends on the community you find yourself in. We are a part of the natural world like all other animals, needing to balance our cooperative and competitive urges. And the evidence suggests we sit at the better end of that range far more often than we might think.

Now that we know how central touch and cooperation are to primates and human nature, I hope we can stop being pessimistic when we predict others’ behavior and motives. A study published in Science this June, covering 125 countries and over 100,000 people, found that 69% of us cooperate with a stranger when given the choice. Asked to guess, people put it at 47%. That pessimism showed up in 124 of the 125 countries surveyed. This matters in the grander scheme of things because those of us who expect others to cooperate are far more likely to cooperate also. When researchers simply told participants that most people worldwide see climate change as a threat, belief in others’ willingness to cooperate ticked up, and actual cooperation followed it, slightly, but in the right direction.

Building on the lessons of primate relationships is easier than it seems.

Seek simple interactions. One of the main ways our primate cousins build affiliative relationships is spending time sitting in close proximity. They may groom, or play, or even sit in contact. More often than not they just like to hang out near their close partners. Just being close to one another is meaningful.

Try a car journey or a five-a-side game. Build trust and relationship through activities where nobody has to look anyone in the eye. If a mate isn’t much of a talker, doing something alongside him might get further than sitting him down and asking how he’s doing.

Reach out before a crisis, not after. Great apes exchange most of their reassurance in the tense minutes before competition, not the wreckage afterward. Reconciliation and comforting are commonplace in humans and primates, but it’s much easier to prevent escalation than it is to smooth things over after a fight.

This piece is part of a three-year GGSC project to explore love's role in promoting social well-being, bridging divides, and contributing to a good, meaningful life.

Don’t wait to be the one who’s approached. That 22-point gap between how we actually cooperate and what we think everyone else will do shows the power of offering an invitation to relationship. Most of us are waiting for someone else to go first.

Influencers selling young men and boys on their primal nature fly in the face of the science and what nature actually looks like. Force and competition are real parts of biology, and something we humans have to manage in our everyday lives. But, if there’s one thing I’ve learned from my many years studying our closest relatives, it’s that touch, care, cooperation, and even love are the most instinctive natural components of being part of the primate family.

Jake Brooker, Ph.D., is an NWO Veni scholar based at Utrecht University, The Netherlands, who studies social cognition and socio-emotional behavior in great apes. He completed doctoral and postdoctoral work at Durham University, U.K.

#9517. 3 Ways to Extinguish Emotional Reactivity

Smoldering flames may reignite. Rather than burying your emotions, try these strategies to minimize and outsmart them.

It starts with a spark — a critical comment, a goal unrealized — and our emotions quickly catch fire. This blaze can be public and palpable, or private and hidden. Spiraling thoughts, avoidance, self-criticism, and other reactive patterns may create a temporary sense of control, but they backfire over time, trapping us in reactivity loops that increase rather than reduce distress. They can also paralyze us.

When distressing emotions threaten to consume you, try the strategies below to neutralize or dampen them.

Observation, or mindful attention, is a foundational skill for emotional regulation because it creates a pause between stimulus and response.

To build this skill, alternate between focusing on your breath and on how your emotions live in your body – rapid heartbeat, knots in your stomach, tight fists, etc. Then expand your focus: What sights and sounds near and far do you notice? Now bring your attention back to your breath.

Fight the impulse to stuff down your emotions, as unpleasant or distressing as they may feel. For helpful cues, try saying “allow” aloud or picturing a green light through which your emotions can pass.

[Read: 7 Truths About ADHD and Intense Emotions]

Try these visual exercises to buy yourself even more time to process emotions. Imagine…

[Read: Why We Feel So Much — and Ways to Overcome It]

Shifting how you view a situation can modify your emotional response to it. Keep these reframing statements somewhere close and read them in moments of distress:

Over time, these skills will help you gain emotional clarity and choose actions that align with your values, not your reactive urges. In practice, that might mean taking a risk despite anxiety, putting the phone down instead of sending an angry text, forcing yourself to take a walk instead of isolating, or delaying gratification.

Douglas Mennin, Ph.D., is a professor of clinical psychology at Teachers College, Columbia University, in New York City.

#9516. Rising Fentanyl Use Challenges Current Methadone Induction Protocols

An increasing number of PAs and nurse practitioners (NPs) are working in addiction medicine including opioid treatment programs (OTPs) where they are increasingly able to practice autonomously. A recently released commentary in the Journal of Substance Abuse Treatment highlights the challenges that practitioners at OTPs face in reaching therapeutic doses of methadone for patients who are using fentanyl instead of heroin.1 The commentary authors noted that with “fentanyl’s increased potency when compared to other opioids, many papers have described the need for higher doses of methadone to achieve the therapeutic goal of reducing and suppressing opioid withdrawal and subsequent illicit ongoing fentanyl use.”

The commentary authors make several key observations and related recommendations. One key finding is that patients using fentanyl who enter OTPs may view the increased time needed to achieve an effective dose of methadone as evidence that methadone treatment will not work for them, and that this may serve as yet another barrier to treatment.

Current guidelines for methadone treatment by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) recommend a maximum initial dose of 30 mg per federal OTP regulations, which were established before synthetic opioids became the leading cause of opioid-involved deaths in the United States. Guidelines state that the dose may be increased by 5 mg to 10 mg every 3 to 5 days. This dosing schedule may be ineffective for patients using fentanyl given their higher tolerance; it may take up to a month or more to reach an effective methadone dose in these patients.

The commentary authors offer several points to consider when adapting induction protocols to meet the therapeutic needs of patients using fentanyl and noted that change can be achieved without lengthy regulatory reform. The authors offer evidence from several US studies in which a more rapid methadone induction schedule allowed achievement of therapeutic doses more quickly without an increase in the risk for overdose, which is highest risk during the first few weeks of methadone induction in OTP settings.

This evidence indicates that OTP providers are attempting to address these concerns with a variety of induction variations, suggesting that more research focused on patients using fentanyl is needed.

This commentary is valuable in attempting to spur further innovative efforts to adapt the methadone OTP model to meet the challenges presented by the greater potency of fentanyl. Engagement early in induction can be challenging for any patient with opioid use disorder seeking treatment. Even before the rise in fentanyl use, many patients with opioid use disorder struggled with the induction period when they were initiated on doses that do little early on to suppress withdrawal symptoms, which are common. This problem is even greater now with the rise in fentanyl use, and this commentary demonstrates the need for OTPs to offer a model for how OTPs and OTP regulators can design more effective induction protocols that are both safe and effective.

This article originally appeared on Clinical Advisor

Buresh M, Nahvi S, Steiger S, Weinstein ZM. Adapting methadone inductions to the fentanyl era. J Subst Abuse Treat. 2022;141:108832. doi:10.1016/j.jsat.2022.108832

#9513. Study: Narcolepsy Medication Found to Improve Adult ADHD Symptoms

The orexin 2 receptor agonist called ALKS 7290 parallels stimulants’ path as a narcolepsy medication that evolved into an ADHD treatment.

An investigational narcolepsy medication called ALKS 7290, an orexin 2 receptor (OX2R) agonist, offers a new therapeutic approach for ADHD, according to results from a recent Phase 1B proof-of-concept study. ALKS 7290 is the first OX2R agonist to demonstrate clinically meaningful improvements in ADHD symptoms in adults with the condition, according to the drug’s manufacturer Alkermes plc.1

“OX2R agonists will represent an entirely new class of ADHD treatment, breaking the traditional barrier between stimulants and non-stimulant treatment,” says Greg Mattingly, M.D., a consultant on the Phase 1 and upcoming Phase 2 trials.

Stimulants remain a first-line treatment for ADHD in adults. However, not all patients tolerate the side effects of or see benefits from stimulant medications. According to an ADDitude survey of more than 11,000 adults with ADHD, 78% of respondents taking amphetamines and 70% of those taking methylphenidate experienced some side effects, compared to 66% of adults taking non-stimulant medications.

The drug works by selectively binding to and activating orexin type 2 receptors, proteins in the brain that regulate alertness, arousal, and appetite. This targeted approach could minimize potential side effects and drug misuse, according to Mattingly.

“Unlike traditional stimulants, orexin 2 receptor agonists have no direct effect on dopamine reuptake or release,” says Mattingly, Associate Clinical Professor in the Department of Psychiatry at the Washington University School of Medicine. “Orexin 2 receptor agonists modulate pathways in the brain that are associated with vigilance, reward, and alertness while decreasing impulsivity. By minimizing direct effects on dopamine reuptake or release, they are considered to have a lower abuse potential.”

The two-week double-blind, parallel-group trial included 50 adults with ADHD and 88 adults without. Participants with ADHD were randomly assigned to receive ALKS 7290 at a total daily dose of 20 mg or 50 mg in split doses or placebo.

As early as day six, patients taking ALKS 7290 demonstrated clinically meaningful improvements in ADHD symptoms, as measured by the Adult ADHD Investigator Symptom Rating Scale (AISRS), and in overall ADHD severity, as measured on the Clinical Global Impression-Severity Scale (CGI-S).

By day 14, treatment with ALKS 7290 reduced median baseline AISRS total scores by 14 points for the 20 mg dose and 19 points for the 50 mg dose. Median CGI-S scores declined by one point with the 20-mg dose and two points with the 50-mg dose.

ALKS 7290 was generally well tolerated at both doses, with mild side effects including insomnia, dizziness, change in sustained attention, and constipation.

The ORX2 agonist also shows promise in treating narcolepsy type 1 (NT1), a common co-occurring condition with ADHD. (Approximately 25% of people with narcolepsy have ADHD.).2 In August, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved Orzeyful (oveporexton), a first-in-class OX2R agonist tablet indicated to treat narcolepsy type l (NT1) in adults.3 Takeda Pharmaceuticals, Orzeyful’s manufacturer, expects the drug to be available in November 2026, pending DEA scheduling.

NT1 is a chronic sleep disorder, characterized by excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS), sudden sleep attacks, cataplexy, and sleep disruptions, resulting from a deficiency in orexin-producing neurons.4

ADHD and narcolepsy share several overlapping symptoms related to arousal and wakefulness. Before becoming standard ADHD treatment, stimulants like amphetamine and methylphenidate were used to treat excessive daytime sleepiness found in narcolepsy patients.5

“Our longest surveillance of the safety of amphetamine comes from following people with narcolepsy for their entire lives,” says ADHD expert William Dodson, M.D., LF-APA. Today, Ritalin (methylphenidate) and Adderall (amphetamine) are both central nervous system stimulant medications approved for the treatment of ADHD and narcolepsy in adults and children.

While it is too soon to know if the OX2R agonist used to treat narcolepsy will likewise evolve into a standard ADHD treatment, the parallels to stimulant medications are clear.

“What’s exciting for clinicians was the fact that ALKS 7290 had dose-related improvement in ADHD symptoms with dramatic improvement seen early and sustained throughout the two-week study,” says Mattingly, founding partner of St. Charles Psychiatric Associates. “While preliminary, the level of improvement obtained with this molecule after two weeks was similar to what is typically seen after four to six weeks in a trial of methylphenidate or amphetamine molecules for ADHD treatment.”

Results from a Phase 2 clinical trial evaluating the efficacy and safety of ALKS 7290 in adults with ADHD are expected in 2027.

1 Alkermes Announces Positive Phase 1b Results Demonstrating Clinical Proof-of-Concept for ALKS 7290 in Adults With Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). Press Release. September 21, 2026. Accessed October 15, 2026. https://investor.alkermes.com/news-releases/news-release-details/alkermes-announces-positive-phase-1b-results-demonstrating

2 Ren, Jiafeng, Zhao, Xianchao, Su, Changjun, et. al. (2024). ADHD in narcolepsy: A closer look at prevalence and ties. Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neubiorev.2023.105471

3 FDA Approves First Drug to Treat the Full Range of Narcolepsy Type 1 Symptoms. Press Release. August 5, 2026. Accessed October 15, 2026. https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-approves-first-drug-treat-full-range-narcolepsy-type-1-symptoms

4 Krahn, L.E., Zee, P.C., Thorpy, M.J. (2022) Current understanding of narcolepsy 1 and its comorbidities: what clinicians need to know now. Adv Ther. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12325-021-01992-4

5 Konofal, Eric. (2024). From past to future: 50 years of pharmacological interventions to treat narcolepsy. Pharmacology Biochemistry and Behavior. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pbb.2024.173804

#9512. 17 Ideas From Educators to Start the School Year With Joy

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Joy! What a beautiful way to start the school year, not only because it feels good, but also because science shows that joy is linked closely to learning, as well as individual and collective flourishing.

We asked Greater Good Education newsletter readers to share a favorite strategy for bringing joy into their school or classroom at the beginning of the year. The responses did not disappoint! Here are a few that span ages, time commitments, and subject areas.

Laura M. (Newark, DE): “Dancing it out” is a strategy that has been shown to reduce stress, release held feelings, and encourage kids to be in the moment. Providing time for activities like dancing is often seen as an “extra.” Building this activity into our weekly schedule has become a favorite stress-relieving activity—adding tremendous joy and connection between children and children and children and teachers.

Related Greater Good in Education (GGiE) practices: The World Is a Dance; Getting to Know Each Other Through Dance; We Are Better Dancing Together

Josh (New Haven, CT): Every Monday morning meeting, students greet each other by asking, “What brought you joy (made you smile/laugh) over the weekend?”

Laura H.: At the end of the day, with second graders, we share the activity from our day that brought the most joy. If I wasn’t there for it (i.e., recess, music, art, PE), I ask them to include details.

Related GGiE practices: Noticing Kindness; Giving Thanks; Looking for Gratitude in School; Sharing Gratitude Stories

Emi (Lobitos, Peru): Identifying forms of enchantment—I use this approach in our Women & Water Program. It’s an all-girls (ages 3–16) surf, science, and storytelling program based in Lobitos, a tiny fishing village in Northern Peru. We use “enchantment” as a way for young girls to foster their curiosity, creativity, and care for themselves, peers, community, and the coastal environment. We do this through photography (taking “macro” photos of small, wondrous things found in their environment, like a flower petal, a beetle, etc.). Or we do this in surfing—the girls notice the “awe” of riding the energy of a leftover storm until it crashes into the sand. These girls also made this song after an oil spill that rocked our community about two years ago.

Related GGiE practices: Meaningful Photos for Students; Mindfully Finding Awe in Nature

Angela (Pleasant Hill, CA): I am a school counselor and with my students who experience anxiety we use sidewalk chalk to write positive welcoming messages and pictures in front of our school. It makes others feel welcomed and helps my students feel connected to our school. They even told me it helps get them to school the first couple of days knowing they would see their chalk messages.

Related GGiE practices: Designing the Classroom to Promote Kindness; Kindness Buddy; Awe-Inspiring Affirmations

Lorien (St. Louis, MO): Have a “Would you rather…?” question on the whiteboard at the start of class—the funnier the better. Students put a checkmark next to their choice. It’s a fun way to welcome the “whole student self” into the classroom, not just their “learner selves.” Sometimes we talk about it, but often, we don’t.

Pam (Muscogee County, GA): To kick off the year, my eighth graders design and build a cardboard maze that guides three different rolling spheres from start to finish. Working in teams of four, students sketch a plan, build it with cardboard and hot glue, test it, and revise their design. Nothing works perfectly the first time. Students quickly discover that failure is a useful part of the design process. By the end of the week, teams are cheering when a ping pong ball, golf ball, or rubber ball finally makes it all the way through, and that joy comes from earning it through real trial and error. It sets the tone for the whole year: Engineering is a process of building, testing, and improving.

Kimberly (Williamsport, PA): Something that I introduce during the first week of classes is our 3 Good Things or 3 Little Wins Padlet. Each week students post about three good things or little wins they had during the week. Before the first post, we discuss why it is important to celebrate these things, no matter how small (e.g., a good cup of coffee!). We also discuss the impact that reflecting on these things has on our physical and psychological well-being. Each week I also post my wins for the week and comment on student posts as well. It creates a wonderful community!

Related GGIE practices: Three Good Things for Students; Gratitude Journals

Jonah (Duxbury, VT): As a high school English teacher, the first writing assignment I give to students asks them to choose a (clean) song that represents them and tell me why they feel connected to this song. I then make a playlist including all the students’ songs, and play it during work times or use it to play students’ walk-up song on special days like birthdays.

Related GGiE practices: Creating Musical Playlists for the Classroom; Prosocial Music Hub (13 practices to bring music into the classroom)

Joe (Bridgeport, CT): Students interact with each other as they navigate around the crowded classroom, connected only by cake-pop sticks balanced between each other using only their index finger. Fosters concentration, cooperation, joyful failures, interconnectedness, and intimacy without actually touching one another.

David (San Antonio, TX): For my introductory geology class, I work with the students to develop rules for a “rock-rock-rock” (igneous-sedimentary-metamorphic) version of “rock-paper-scissors.” Students develop the necessary hand signals and the action verbs that say what beats what. Once we have the rules established, the students engage in a best two out of three to crown the class champion. Branded university swag is available for the winners, and everyone gets a candy treat for participating.

Related GGiE practice: Making Science Meaningful

Susan (St. Paul, MN): I ask students to tell the rest of the class their name and a ridiculous lie about themselves—the more absurd the better. There’s always good-natured laughter and encouragement.

Harry (Hailey, ID): I work to end every “session” (class, administration meeting, faculty meeting, etc.) with laughter, whether incited by me or coming from someone else. That moment becomes the punctuation.

Related GGiE practices: Share a Laugh; The SEL 3 Signature Practices

Paige (Seattle, WA): About the second or third week of classes (graduate and undergraduate students) we begin doing this ritual that we do a few times during the semester: “The joy of contribution…I see this in you!” Students take turns identifying something they have genuinely observed in another student in the cohort/class: “One leadership capacity I see developing in you is________, because I watched you ________.” The BECAUSE matters.

Explore compassion, self-compassion, and awe with educators around the world.

Examples I have heard from pre-certified teachers and principals: “I see courage building in you because I have watched you ask questions the rest of us were afraid to ask.” OR, “I see you really owning belongingness as you consistently notice who is outside the conversation and what is happening around us as you read the room.”

Related GGiE practices: I See You. Everyone Matters; Behind Your Back

Lorien (St. Louis, MO): I use a guided visualization to prompt students to think about what joyful teaching, joyful learning, and joyful interactions look like, sound like, and feel like. It makes what we’re doing much more explicit, and it helps me know what they want from me and vice versa.

Related GGiE practice: Designing the Classroom to Promote Kindness

Angela (McMinnville, OR): A non-dominant hand drawing activity that gets us all out of our “perfection” thinking and into being learners…and laughing.

Related GGiE practice: Drawing as a Way to Manage Emotions

Milton (San Diego, CA): As the associate principal, I stand out in front of the school in the morning with a BIG SMILE sign on and greet the students with a “Good morning & have a great day!” Some students like a fist bump or handshake as well.

Related GGiE practice: Making Families Feel Welcome

Donna (Arkansas): “JOY” is the grounding rhythm that closes every day, honoring the joyful moments that JUST happened, recognizing community attunement through something an OTHER person did, and celebrating internal self-efficacy via something YOU did. Each person is free to select whichever letter resonates with them to share. We pass a rainstick around the circle; once it is turned to let its gentle cascade settle into silence, the person holding it speaks. This tactile ritual and quiet sound not only brings a profound sense of calm to the transition from classroom to home, but it also serves as a gentle reminder to carry those reflections outward.

Related GGiE practices: Inspiring Virtue With Moral Beauty; Stories of Moral Beauty; Noticing Kindness; Nurturing Students’ Wonder and Curiosity

Thank you to all of the educators in the Greater Good community who shared activities for bringing joy into schools and classrooms. We received many, many more than we could share here. Even in the face of incredible challenges, you are bringing so much joy to your students and their families, your colleagues, and yourself. May you all have a joyful start to the new school year!

We look forward to our next post in the From Our Readers series that will focus on building community through connection and belonging. Want to share an activity? Fill out this quick form! Not only will you strengthen our community, you’ll be entered into a drawing for a free self-paced course or a spot in our Flourishing Spring community of practice!

#9511. Cheesy Vegan Enchilada Skillet (30 Minutes!)

Disclosure: This post may contain affiliate links which provide us a small commission when used for purchase. We're grateful for your support!

Everything you love about enchiladas, minus the fuss! This super flavorful, cheesy vegan enchilada skillet comes together in about 30 minutes with simple methods, minimal dishes, and no need to fill or roll tortillas.

This easy, nourishing dish features tender cubed sweet potato or winter squash, fiber- & protein-rich black beans, and a rich red enchilada sauce. Everything gets simmered in 1 pan and topped with a melty cashew “cheese” that makes it SUPER satisfying and delicious!

It’s believed that enchiladas may have originated from a similar Mayan dish called papadzules. But the first written recipe for enchiladas was in an 1831 cookbook called El Cocinero mexicano. Typically, enchiladas are made with meat, seafood, beans, cheese, potatoes, or vegetables stuffed in corn tortillas and topped with enchilada sauce.

Our “inspired-by” enchilada skillet has all the flavors of classic enchiladas, but it’s vegan, and instead of rolling the filling in tortillas, we slice the tortillas and cook everything together in one pan on the stovetop!

This 1-pan, 30-minute vegan enchilada skillet begins with a base of sautéed vegetables — onion, garlic, sweet potato, and poblano pepper. The veggies are flexible here, so feel free to experiment! We love kabocha squash for a fall variation and have found green bell peppers work well when poblanos aren’t available. We also think butternut squash would be nice, as would greens such as kale or spinach.

Once the onions are very tender and the squash and peppers are just beginning to soften, we stir in black beans + corn tortillas that have been sliced into strips.

Next comes the final ingredient in the skillet portion of this dish (hello, simple + flavorful!): red enchilada sauce. We love the bold flavor of our homemade enchilada sauce (and usually have it stocked in the freezer), but this recipe also works well with store-bought enchilada sauce.

And lastly, it just wouldn’t be enchiladas without: the CHEESE! More specifically, a flavorful cashew “cheese” sauce inspired by our fan favorite Cheesy Vegan Pizza Beans. It’s made by blending up cashews, water, lime juice, garlic, tapioca starch, and sea salt. When poured over the enchilada skillet and covered with a lid, the heat and tapioca starch do their magic, creating a melty, cheesy layer! Total swoon!

We highly recommend trying the cashew “cheese” sauce, even if you’re not vegan or dairy-free! It’s super easy and takes this dish to a whole new level. However, this enchilada skillet is also delicious with shredded vegan or dairy cheese (such as pepper jack).

We think you’ll LOVE this recipe! It’s:SmokySpicySuper flavorfulSatisfyingVersatileQuick & easy to make& SO delicious!

This dish is hearty and amazing as a standalone quick meal for weeknights! It would also pair well with our Smoky Shredded Tofu Taco “Meat” or 1-Pan Mexican Shredded Chicken for a higher-protein option. Or, for more veggies, try it with our Crunchy Jicama Slaw or Quick Citrusy Cabbage Slaw.

If you try this recipe, let us know! Leave a comment, rate it, and don’t forget to tag a photo @minimalistbaker on Instagram. Cheers, friends!

Tag @minimalistbaker on Instagram and hashtag it #minimalistbaker so we can see all the deliciousness!FacebookTwitterPin It

#9510. ADHD Lacks a Biomarker Test… But Not Scientific Validity

ADHD’s validity is confirmed not by a blood test but by an overwhelming convergence of scientific evidence, including a reliable behavioral phenotype, genetic heritability, measurable life impairments, and more.

The diagnostic legitimacy of ADHD has been vigorously debated in contemporary psychiatry circles. For parents navigating a child’s diagnosis or adults receiving a later-in-life diagnosis, the central paradox is this: ADHD has profound, life-altering symptoms but no definitive biological test, such as a blood panel or a brain scan, to confirm its presence.

This absence of biomarkers is frequently cited by critics who characterize ADHD as a modern social construct, a byproduct of high-pressure academic environments, or a medicalization of normal childhood energy. However, the scientific consensus, codified in the 2021 World Federation of ADHD International Consensus Statements, asserts that ADHD is a valid, highly heritable, and neurobiologically grounded disorder.1

In modern medicine, the gold standard for disease validation is a typically quantifiable, objective indicator of a biological state. When you are sick or injured, you expect a physician to draw blood, perform a biopsy, or order a scan or some other laboratory test. Because this reliance on objective evidence is so deeply ingrained, skeptics and critics of ADHD point to the absence of a definitive biomarker as evidence of its illegitimacy. However, these critics misunderstand (or intentionally ignore) this well-known fact: Many indisputably valid disorders cannot be affirmed with biomarker tests.

In fact, painful and disabling disorders such as migraine headaches, trigeminal neuralgia, myalgic encephalomyelitis, complex regional pain syndrome, interstitial cystitis, and mild traumatic brain injury are indisputably physical, nonpsychiatric medical diseases without biomarkers. What these critics ignore is that most, if not all, nonpsychiatric medical disorders were viewed as disorders long before a biomarker test was available.

Medical science says that we observe suffering, seek to understand its causes and treatments, and ideally, find a biomarker for diagnosis. But in the absence of a biomarker, we still must help those in need.

[Get This Free Download: Unraveling the Mysteries of Your ADHD Brain]

Critics of ADHD as a diagnosis also ignore the fact that psychiatric science has established criteria for what is, and what is not, a disorder. In a 2005 paper, “The Scientific Foundation for Understanding Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder as a Valid Psychiatric Disorder,” I documented how ADHD meets all these criteria.2 Below is a summary.

Does ADHD have a consistent and recognizable pattern of symptoms and functional impairments? Yes. Inattention, impulsivity, and hyperactivity are well defined, and those with ADHD have clear functional impairments, ranging from severe academic problems and poor peer relations to accidental injuries and occupational failure. A trait becomes a disorder when it is associated with significant distress or disability, and most people with ADHD would agree that their condition brings both.

Does ADHD have objective correlates, such as neuroimaging, psychological testing, or biochemical markers? Indeed, many studies have documented impaired performance on neuropsychological tests, small differences in brain structure and function, and genetic variants that increase risk for ADHD. This criterion does not require the correlates to be useful for diagnosis, only that they are more likely to be observed in those with the condition compared to those without.

Though individuals with ADHD are at higher risk for other disorders, the symptoms used to diagnose ADHD are different from those used to diagnose commonly coexisting disorders such as anxiety and mood disorders.

[Get This Free Download: Fight Misinformation with These 11 Facts About ADHD]

Does ADHD have a trajectory across the lifespan? Yes, the continuation of symptoms from childhood to adulthood and the emergence of other disorders associated with ADHD have been well documented.

Is there evidence of a genetic cause for ADHD? Yes, ADHD has high heritability and DNA studies show that most cases of ADHD are caused by the accumulation of many genetic risk variants.

Does ADHD have a predictable and beneficial response to specific therapeutic interventions? Yes, substantial evidence supports the benefit of stimulant and non-stimulant medications as well as parent behavior therapy for children and cognitive behavioral therapy for adults.

ADHD’s existence is undeniable. The application of these criteria to ADHD provides a rigorous scientific defense against the claim that the disorder is merely a collection of subjective labels. Its validity is established, not by a simple lab or blood test, but by an overwhelming convergence of scientific evidence: a highly reliable behavioral phenotype, strong genetic heritability, distinct population-level neurobiological correlates, severe and measurable life impairments, and a clear response to medical and psychological treatments. Waiting for a perfect biomarker while children and adults suffer preventable harms would abandon medical responsibility.

Stephen V. Faraone, Ph.D., is a distinguished professor of psychiatry at SUNY Upstate Medical University. He is the founder of the ADHDEvidenceProject.org.

#9508. The Everyday Nutrient Linked To 32% Lower Dementia Risk

Your brain uses this nutrient for memory, but its relationship with dementia risk is more complicated than “more is better”.

Your brain uses this nutrient for memory, but its relationship with dementia risk is more complicated than “more is better”.

Moderate intake of choline, a nutrient found in eggs, fish and legumes, is linked to a lower risk of dementia.

Older adults consuming moderately high amounts had a 32 percent lower dementia risk than those consuming the least.

However, the highest intake was not associated with a clear benefit, suggesting that more is not necessarily better.

The research followed over 5,000 American adults, whose average age was almost 69, for around eight years.

Participants were initially free of dementia but around 500 developed the condition during follow-up.

After dividing participants into five groups according to choline intake, the researchers found a 32 percent lower dementia risk in the second-highest group than in the lowest, after accounting for other factors.

However, there was no statistically clear reduction in the highest-intake group.

The result therefore points towards a potentially beneficial range, rather than a steady fall in risk with every increase in consumption.

The researchers then combined their results with four previous studies to assess the broader pattern.

Together, these followed almost 138,000 people and recorded around 2,500 cases of dementia.

In the combined analysis, dementia risk fell as choline intake rose to approximately 465 milligrams per day, with no further reduction beyond that level.

Choline helps the brain produce acetylcholine, a chemical messenger involved in learning and memory.

It also supplies building blocks for the membranes surrounding brain cells, helping maintain their structure and communication.

These roles could help explain a link between choline and cognitive ageing, although they do not prove that consuming more prevents dementia.

The nutrient also participates in processes that regulate homocysteine, a substance linked to problems with blood vessels and cognitive function.

Eggs, meat, poultry and nuts were among the main sources of choline in the American participants’ diets.

People consuming more choline obtained a greater proportion of it from eggs.

Crucially, the analysis assessed choline from food and did not include intake from supplements.

The findings therefore cannot establish whether choline supplements would lower dementia risk.

The study was published in the Nutrition Journal (Chen et al., 2026).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9507. ADHD and the Social Processing Gap

“There’s a difference between having social skills and being able to use them consistently in the moment. This is the fundamental challenge for people living with ADHD.”

“Knowing social expectations versus implementing them in real time is a very big challenge for people with ADHD.” — Sharon Saline, Psy.D.

This tension is at the heart of many slip-ups — from oversharing and interrupting to difficulties reading the room — that stump adults with ADHD across various scenarios. Dr. Saline, a clinical psychologist who specializes in ADHD, described this as the “social processing gap” during her October ADDitude webinar, “Reading Body Language & Social Cues: A Primer for People with ADHD.”

Here, learn more about the gap and how to fill it, along with quick tips for navigating sticky social situations with ease and confidence.

ADHD symptoms and traits — like working memory challenges, distractibility, impulsivity, hyperfocus and more — directly impact communication and social skills. But there’s another factor that tends to influence social interactions: shame.

We asked: Which of the following social challenges prompted you to be here today — for yourself or someone important to you? (Select all that apply.)

A history of negative and uncomfortable social interactions means that many adults with ADHD approach social situations assuming they’ll misread a facial expression, take up too much of the conversation, or commit a faux pas. As a result, many are unable to fully participate in conversations without extreme vigilance and/or becoming overwhelmed, anxious, self-conscious, or exhausted.

“ADHD affects our ability to interpret social information when it’s occurring in real time, because of anxiety and rejection sensitivity that complicate those interpretations and how people respond,” Saline said.

Navigating misunderstandings in relationships, friendships, family, and work comes down to three words: Notice. Check. Clarify.

Noticing, or building social awareness, doesn’t mean scanning for signs of disapproval. It is being attuned to other people and adapting to connection, without taking things too personally or making assumptions. “The challenge is to notice these cues without automatically assuming that they’re bored, annoyed, or rejecting us,” Saline said.

That’s where clarification comes in. Uncertainty is a potent trigger for rejection sensitivity, so Saline encourages respectful questioning to address assumptions. For example, if your partner says they’re not upset but their tone sounds irritated, ask, “I’m hearing something different in your tone. Is there something you’d like to talk about?”

#9505. How to Build a Habit by Starting Ridiculously Small

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

In 75 minutes a week, I can reap the benefits of listening to uplifting music, getting out in nature, and getting morning outdoor light, all while exercising my dogs and getting enough cardio to measurably improve my health, happiness, and longevity.

And at times in my life, I have been a real runner. I ran a marathon in my 20s and a couple of half-marathons in my 30s. In my 40s, I mostly just made spectacular plans every January and September: I’d find exciting destination races to train for, join a gym and a yoga studio, sign up for running challenges, and pick out elaborate training plans. I’d run three or four days a week for a week or two, and then nada. Zippo. Zero runs per week.

Then, in 2020, I got into a real running habit. I’ve told the longer version of this story on a TED stage, so I won’t repeat it here, but suffice it to say that I did it by doing very, very little running. When I started going to Orange Theory classes, I kept running. I sustained this exercise habit for six years, through breast cancer and many other difficult life events.

Then the Orange Theory studio down the street from me closed. I tried other studios, but the classes I like are impossible to get into.

So I embraced working out on my own and getting back to running outside with my dogs. I bought very heavy dumbbells and set up a home gym on our covered porch. I spent an inordinate amount of time choosing a destination race, enlisting my adult children to join me. I set up a training schedule on my Garmin watch, and when I didn’t stick to it, I used Nike Run Club. I made a running playlist. I bought a double running leash.

Friends, I have done four runs in three weeks.

I know what I need to do. It’s so wildly unambitious that I’m embarrassed to tell you. I just need to get dressed to run first thing in the morning, put my dogs on their double leash, put on my playlist, and walk out the door, down the driveway, and to the mailbox. That’s it.

I know that most days, I’ll get a walk in, and once that walk is familiar, I’ll sometimes run a little. Some days I might run more, without even deciding to. But even when I don’t feel like doing more, the morning light I get while retrieving the mail and the walk back up our steep driveway are both good for me and genuinely enjoyable. It’s way better than nothing.

The mistake I make again and again is assuming that the size of my plan and the odds of my success are related: the more inspiring the goal and the more elaborate the plan, the better my results will be.

Ambition and results are related, of course, but not in the direction you think.

Creating a habit takes energy and focus, and we’ve only got so much of either, which is why ambitious plans produce a brilliant week and then…nothing. It takes between 18 and 254 days for a behavior to become automatic, and what predicts faster adoption isn’t ambition, self-discipline, or willpower; it’s repetition.

Repetition in a consistent context drives habit formation. Not just effort, intensity, or how badly someone wants it. Doing the thing, in the same place at about the same time, again and again, has the most impact.

Eli Susman, Ph.D., joins me in a webinar in a few weeks to talk about his book Micropractice.

Microhabits: The Science of Habits So Small They Actually Stick

Success is motivating. Doing what you said you’d do, even something absurdly small, builds the belief that you can do it. Failing repeatedly does the opposite; that’s a big part of why I spent my 40s making elaborate plans but not running.

Small behaviors make repetition more likely. What separates an actual habit from a nice couple of weeks is whether it holds up when you’re stressed, tired, busy, or not feeling 100%.

Missing a single day doesn’t meaningfully set most people back. We don’t need to be perfect here, folks. What won’t survive is a plan so ambitious that the off days outnumber the on days.

Micropractices, as researcher Eli Susman calls them, are very small behaviors that also have their own benefits; a tiny practice isn’t just a placeholder for a “real” one. Susman found that 20 seconds of self-compassionate touch (for example, sending kindness to yourself while placing your hand on your heart) per day improved mental health and lowered stress compared with a placebo finger tapping practice.

Across 280,000 meditation sessions in 103 countries, how consistently people meditated predicted their mood and resilience better than how long they sat. Similarly, a meta-analysis combining the results of many studies found that the benefits of practicing breathwork for stress didn’t depend on how long the session were. And breaking up six hours of sitting with brief bouts of walking improves energy, mood, and food cravings more than doing 30 minutes of walking all at once.

I hate the idea of abandoning my big plans. But the truth is that I am not choosing between the ambitious version and the tiny version. I am choosing between the tiny version and nothing.

Break the core behavior central to your habit down into something you can do in under five minutes, start to finish. Under a minute is even better. This isn’t the version that would impress your doctor or your neighbors; it’s the version you can do while exhausted, while traveling, while a little bit sick, and when you want nothing more than to stay on the couch.

Then, check it for resistance. If you feel any reluctance when you imagine doing it, it isn’t small enough yet. Cut it in half. Most people need to start with a micropractice: putting on your walking shoes and stepping out the front door, doing one pushup or 30 seconds of breathing, eating a single leaf of romaine, which, for the record, contains actual fiber and actual nutrients.

Do just that for a while. Resist the urge to do more. This is hard, but the moment you’re no longer willing to be unambitious is the moment you put the whole thing at risk. That’s when difficulty enters, and negotiation with yourself, and the possibility of failure. Your tiny habit doesn’t depend on motivation, which is precisely what makes it survive the days when you have none.

Expand only when you’re itching to, and only in absurdly small increments. Go one more minute, not 10.

Every time you repeat a behavior, your brain physically strengthens the connections that produce it, the way feet crossing a meadow gradually wear a path. Repeat it enough and the path becomes a groove your brain follows on its own, no willpower required. You’re carving a neural pathway for your habit, and everything you want is downstream from that.

At some point, it will become uncomfortable not to do this new behavior. You’ll do it without deciding to, without trying to. That’s the whole goal: repetition until the thing runs itself.

It’s hard to abandon our grand plans and great ambitions for something embarrassingly small. But, paradoxically, it is only in that tiny step that some of our grand plans are truly born.

Join Christine Carter and Eli Susman on Oct. 15 for a free live conversation, with a few tiny habits to try together.

Christine Carter, Ph.D. is a Senior Fellow at the Greater Good Science Center. She is the author of The New Adolescence: Raising Happy and Successful Teens in an Age of Anxiety and Distraction (BenBella, 2020), The Sweet Spot: How to Accomplish More by Doing Less (Ballantine Books, 2015), and Raising Happiness: 10 Simple Steps for More Joyful Kids and Happier Parents (Random House, 2010). A former director of the GGSC, she served for many years as author of its parenting blog, Raising Happiness. Find out more about Christine here.

#9501. Increased Risk for Suicide Attempts Among Children Who Use Tobacco Products

Children who report the use of tobacco products — including e-cigarettes and vaping — have a 3 to 5 times increased risk for suicide attempts (SAs), according to study results published in JAMA Network Open.

New tobacco products (ie, e-cigarettes, vapes, hookahs) have become increasingly popular in the United States, particularly among children and adolescents. Although it is well-documented that adolescents and adults who smoke cigarettes have an increased likelihood of suicidality, it is unclear whether this heightened risk applies to children who use tobacco products.

To address this knowledge gap, researchers conducted a cross-sectional cohort study from September 1 to September 5, 2022. The researchers used data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study, a nationally representative cohort of 11,868 US children enrolled at 9 and 10 years of age. The objective of the current study was to investigate the correlation between tobacco product use and the incidence of nonsuicidal self-injury (NSSI), suicidal ideation (SI), and SAs among preadolescent children. Substance use was evaluated using the ABCD Youth Substance Use Interview and hair toxicology tests at baseline, a 6-month follow-up, and then yearly. The researchers assessed suicidality using children and caregiver reports of the Kiddie Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia (K-SADS-5).

The researchers included data from 8988 children (median age, 9.8 years; 47.9% girls). At baseline, 1.1% of children reported ever using tobacco products, and this prevalence rose significantly to 1.7% at the 18-month follow-up. The researchers observed no statistical difference in smoking experience by sex or race/ethnicity; however, tobacco-using children generally came from more socioeconomically disadvantaged backgrounds, had greater prenatal smoking exposure, and were more likely to have parents with a history of depression, alcohol issues, and behavioral or suicide-related problems, relative to children who did not use tobacco products.

The researchers observed significant associations between tobacco product use among children and increased risks for SAs at each time point. Tobacco use was linked to a 3 to 5 times higher risk for SAs, with an odds ratio (OR) of 4.67 (95% CI, 2.35-9.27; P <.001) at baseline, 4.25 (95% CI, 2.33-7.74; P <.001) at 1 year, and 2.85 (95% CI, 1.58-5.12; P =.001) at year 2.

The researchers also evaluated whether children’s personality, cognition, and psychological outcomes were associated with tobacco product use. They found that children were more likely to endorse tobacco use if they had conduct disorder (P <.001), oppositional defiant disorder (P <.001), rule-breaking behaviors (P <.001), aggressive behaviors (P <.001), social problems (P =.009), attention problems (P =.02), as well as personality traits of lack of planning (P <.001), positive urgency (P =.006), lack of perseverance (P =.009), sensation seeking (P =.02), aggression (P =.02), negative urgency (P =.03), and depressive mood (P <.05).

However, the association between tobacco use and SAs remained elevated, independent of these behavioral/psychopathology traits (OR, 3.09; 95% CI, 1.70-5.65; P <.001) in regression analyses. Conversely, the association between tobacco use and SI was not sustained when childhood behavioral measures were considered.

Among other substance use, only alcohol sipping was independently associated with SAs (OR, 1.55; 95% CI, 1.14-2.13; P =.007). These findings suggest that while other substance use is related to SAs, tobacco product use remains a robust independent risk factor.

Study authors concluded, “The findings suggest that smoking tobacco products may be a modifiable risk factor that can be addressed in suicide prevention efforts, especially among children.”

These study findings may be limited by the use of hair toxicology tests to assess tobacco use and the inability to determine causality, given the observational study design.

Lee PH, Tervo-Clemmens B, Liu RT, et al. Use of tobacco products and suicide attempts among elementary school-aged children. JAMA Netw Open. Published online February 5, 2024. doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.0376

#9500. New Research Strengthens the Case for Emotional Dysregulation in ADHD Criteria

The new “severe-combined” ADHD subtype identified in a landmark study is marked by emotional dysregulation, a symptom the DSM-5 doesn’t include in its diagnostic criteria.

When the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5) was updated in 2022, officials believed that research was lacking to expand ADHD’s definition to include the common and extremely impairing symptom of emotional dysregulation. Consequently, the overwhelming and uncontrollable emotions reported by many patients remain largely unrecognized as ADHD manifestations.

Now research appears to be catching up to patient reports.

A new landmark study has revealed three ADHD subtypes that reflect neurobiological differences: predominantly inattentive; predominantly hyperactive/impulsive; and the new severe-combined, which is marked by emotional dysregulation.1

Using neuroimaging and computational modeling to map the pathways of ADHD, researchers found that the severe-combined type had 45 areas of brain abnormality tied to emotion and control compared with 26 each for the two other types. The study, which analyzed 1,154 brain scans of children and adolescents with ADHD, was published recently in JAMA Psychiatry.

The findings are “an example of recent insights emerging from neuroimaging that may impact clinical care, which has been an elusive goal,” says F. Xavier Castellanos, M.D., professor emeritus of child and adolescent psychiatry at New York University’s Grossman School of Medicine. He was part of the working group that contributed to the DSM-5.

[Get This Free Download: Emotional Regulation & Anger Management Scripts]

“Still, it’s too early to assume that their intriguing results are real in the sense of replicating repeatedly in independent datasets, particularly by investigators who are not allied or collaborating with the original research team,” says Castellanos. He, like the study authors, calls for prospective studies to validate their biotypes and determine whether they may influence treatment.

Findings that reveal a new severe-combined subtype may come as no surprise to the thousands of parents of children with ADHD, and adults with the condition, who have named emotional dysregulation as the most impairing feature of ADHD in ADDitude surveys.

But, as David Anderson, Ph.D., senior psychologist at the ADHD and Behavior Disorders Center at the Child Mind Institute, points out, parents’ anecdotal feedback precedes scientific validation.

“Finding evidence of a subtype in the brain leaves open questions about the balance of nature versus nurture. Is there a biological basis for subtypes and is it reliable across the span of development?” Anderson asks. “Emotion dysregulation can be biological for kids who are more prone to emotional behavior from an early age, while some are frustrated with the world due to negative feedback they’ve gotten since kindergarten, so it’s environmental. There are multiple pathways to come to this.”

[Read: The Key to ADHD Emotional Regulation? Cultivating Gratitude, Pride & Compassion]

If the study’s findings are replicated, Castellanos says, it would become a new presentation in a future version of the DSM. “I served on the DSM-5 committee, and we were explicitly reminded that the DSM follows the field; it does not lead it. It’s only when the scientific evidence is strongly supportive that DSM changes are allowed. Otherwise, it’s too disruptive.”

Stephen V. Faraone, Ph.D., distinguished professor at SUNY Upstate Medical University, said he believes that emotional dysregulation was not included in the DSM-5 because it might have made differential diagnosis with anxiety and mood disorders more difficult, especially in primary care. He also said he was skeptical that ADHD can be divided into biological subtypes, adding that underlying ADHD brain mechanisms exist along a spectrum and do not fall neatly into separate categories.

The study’s researchers said the findings may eventually create a path toward developing personalized therapeutic strategies.

Carole Fleck is Editor-in-Chief at ADDitude magazine.
