#9499. Seven Ways to Outlast Political Authoritarianism

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Though Djurdja Padejski was raised in communist Yugoslavia, her life there felt stable and uneventful for a long time. In the 1980s, under Yugoslavia’s “soft” one-party government, Padejski and her friends read Western literature, watched Hollywood movies, and listened to the BBC.

“We grew up in a very comfortable, naive environment,” Padejski says.

That changed in the 1990s when Yugoslavia split into several republics. Civil war broke out, and a virulent strain of nationalism took hold in Serbia, the Yugoslavian state where Padejski lived. Firebrand leader Slobodan Milošević ascended to power and began meddling in elections, targeting opposition leaders, and igniting ethnic cleansing campaigns.

“He captured the entire society and his party,” Padejski remembers. “Very soon I found myself on the streets protesting.” Padejski’s activism against repressive Serbian regimes would continue until 2011, when she and her husband, investigative journalist Djordje Padejski, left the country after people threatened to kill them.

The Padejskis arrived in the U.S. with hard-won knowledge of how to outlast repression over the long haul. In recent years, they’ve tapped back into that knowledge and shared it with those around them as they witness here in America the illegal destruction of government agencies, election tampering, and warrantless arrests of citizens and non-citizens. This isn’t just true in the United States—around the world, democracy is declining.

How can we go on defying rising authoritarianism when no clear endpoint is in sight? Psychology and motivation research complement the experience of people like the Padejskis by addressing how to conserve energy and sustain commitment to your ideals in challenging conditions.

“The goal of the authoritarian regime is to desensitize us to extremes, to things we should never agree with or consider normal,” says Djurdja Padejski, now a language and culture researcher (and doctoral candidate) at Arizona State University.

Surviving repression depends on rejecting this presumed “normality” and refusing to let your inner state mirror extremes imposed from above. To that end, here are seven research-backed ways to subsist under indefinite duress.

Life under repression feels exhausting due to the colossal scale of so much of what is happening: attacks on the free press, denial of life-saving aid to millions overseas, ongoing ICE killings on the streets and in detention facilities. Reading about such developments understandably triggers feelings of overwhelm. Research finds that these feelings can drive people to shut down their emotions, dampening their motivation to help in concrete ways.

Djurdja Padejski has come to recognize that to avoid that trap, she has to face her human limits squarely without drowning in self-recrimination. As a young adult under Milošević’s rule, she learned early that worrying about what she couldn’t do was a waste of time and energy.

“It is very important not to get stuck in that moment, not to be clutching your pearls,” she says. “We have to be strategic to preserve our resources.”

Admitting your own lack of control over the big picture can be a necessary prelude to taking the actions still available to you, Padejski says. “We have to see [the situation] for what it is, so we can focus our efforts on keeping our minds, our bodies, and our communities as healthy as possible under the circumstances.”

Once you’ve gotten clear about what is within your power to control, you can get granular by carrying out regular acts of “micro-resistance.” These acts of defiance do not require you to upend your daily rhythms or put your life on the line. They can be as simple as attending a march, supporting a neighbor at an immigration court visit, or wearing a shirt with a resistance slogan.

Micro-resistance acts—such as creating protest art and continuing to study even when their department was banned from the university—helped sustain both Padejskis through years of repression, reminding them of the power they had despite limits imposed from on high.

“These micro-level actions add up,” Djordje Padejski writes. “Even small acts of defiance can maintain your sense of agency.”

Self-described “small-time” lawyer Daniel Suitor excels at this kind of micro-resistance. During ICE raids in his hometown of Minneapolis, he channeled his overwhelm by signing up for a course on how to file legal paperwork to free unjustly detained Twin Cities residents.

After Suitor filed his first case, he found out surprisingly quickly that he’d won and that the man he was representing would be freed. That proof-of-concept case spurred him to file another legal petition, then several more in quick succession. And he wasn’t alone in his commitment: To date, Minnesota lawyers have filed more than 1,000 cases challenging unjust detentions.

Acts of micro-resistance can also help prime us for future courageous action. When people perform smaller acts of selflessness and service, large-scale heroism becomes easier to contemplate, explains Medical College of Wisconsin heroism researcher Zeno Franco. Concrete practice can make you more adept at translating abstract ideals into action.

“You need to understand beyond theory,” Djurdja Padejski says. “We actually, as humans, can’t imagine how concepts work in [the] real world unless we experience them hands-on.”

For the Padejskis, one of the most stifling aspects of life under Serbian autocracy was not knowing when the repression would lift, if at all.

Periods of confinement, literal or figurative, are more bearable when a clear endpoint is in sight, and indefinite periods of repression feel uniquely oppressive. A third or more of incarcerated people with open-ended sentences suffer from depression. Others feel rooted to the present moment, severed from any potential future.

“I simply try to live in the here and now and not to plan,” one prisoner told the University of Bern researcher Irene Marti, who studies open-ended confinement. “Because I don’t have any future or only one that is very far away.”

When the endpoint of repression is uncertain, or when a challenging situation has no clear natural limit, creating your own intermediate endpoints can help you stay committed to your goals and values.

In a recent goal-setting study, when people broke an annual community service goal into granular sub-goals (say, four hours of service a week, or eight every two weeks), they volunteered more hours in the long run than people without intermediate goals.

In the same way, committed resisters can pledge to put in a set number of hours each week, or carry out a set number of clearly defined actions. According to self-determination theory, choosing and pursuing your own accessible goals boosts your well-being and motivation—internal changes that persist even when the larger crisis remains ongoing.

As governments around the world curtail freedom of speech and movement, it’s hard not to feel the noose tightening. One way to create more existential breathing room is to consider how this moment fits into the longer arc of history.

This helps you subsist in the present by reminding you of parallel past moments (whether decades or centuries ago), how they came to a head, and what ultimately resolved them. Research finds that when people take a long-term perspective, reflecting on recent stressful events as though they happened far in the past, they report less emotional distress in the moment.

Djurdja Padejski found solace in doing this during Milošević’s reign. “I survived that period mostly by reading the columns in the newspapers,” she says. One column in particular, by Serbian anthropologist Ivan Čolović, examined the regime’s activities from a broader historical and social perspective.

“He was offering a vocabulary and a theoretical apparatus to help us deal with the horrors of civil war. The news about it was the most severely censored, the propaganda was relentless, and all of it was new for many of us who were children when the fallout of our world began,” Padejski says. “That’s how I survived with my sanity intact, because it helped me to recognize what is happening to society.”

Among the most potent present-day energy drains is the social media industrial complex that feeds on people’s rage and frustration, serving up extreme viewpoints that deepen entrenched social divides as they rack up likes and views.

“Social media and internet platforms—they’re amplifying what is also a typical quality of authoritarian regimes. They’re all about grandiosity,” says Djurdja Padejski, who studies the linguistic mechanisms of propaganda. “Algorithms grab people’s attention by intensifying the language and the visuals and the overall framing.” That’s a big reason why frequent social media use saps your cognitive resources and motivation, making it harder to subsist under repression.

Plugging this energy drain requires not just limiting your time online, but redirecting more of that time to the in-person, small-group exchange to which humans are uniquely suited.

When you engage with people face to face, it’s much harder to reduce them to a stereotype or particular viewpoint. And by getting to know them in all their messiness, contradiction, and complexity, you bond with them in ways that lighten the mental and practical load for everyone involved.

“To resist this reduction of our existence to, ‘What are you for or against?’ means embracing creativity, art, friends, communal projects, protests, walks,” Padejski says. “These 10 years of resistance [in Serbia]—I honestly remember it as a series of walks. Sometimes that meant running away together from Milošević‘s militias or the official police, or from water cannons, or rubber bullets. But what is left is our conversations on ideas, on creations.”

Though exchanges like these may not further resistance directly, they form the edifice that sustains it. Within bonded human-scale communities, members have a clear sense of not just their own energetic capacity, but that of others in the group. That means they can pinch-hit for one another: When someone needs help, they can fill in on the spot—or, like relay racers, take up the baton when someone needs to withdraw. This shared flexibility and responsiveness help all group members to stay committed for the long haul.

For the Padejskis, subsisting under Serbian repression meant homing in on the values that were most important to them, and upholding those values even if it meant sacrificing convenience or comfort. When Djordje Padejski needed a lifesaving drug, a relative told him he could work his connections to obtain the medicine, but only if Padejski joined the Serbian dictator’s political party. Padejski refused, knowing that doing so put his health at risk.

The couple have continued that tradition in the U.S., though in somewhat less life-altering ways. After Elon Musk unleashed an apparent Nazi salute at a Trump post-inauguration event, the Padejskis gave up their Tesla. “I drive a Subaru now,” Djurdja Padejski says. “I really don’t like it compared to Tesla, but I don’t regret it.”

Some people write off such moral stands as more symbolic than substantive. But symbol, it turns out, shapes substance: What you stand for predicts and influences what you’ll do down the road, for good or ill. When people have a clear, consistent moral identity, studies find, they’re more likely to take real-world action aligned with that identity.

On the other hand, when you’re willing to cave on something that seems minor, like supporting a complicit business, “you are detached from your inner beliefs, from what you know is real and good and safe,” Djurdja Padejski says. “Once you’re there, you are ready to compromise a lot of values that you think you are really one with.”

One unexpected thing the Padejskis learned, under Milošević and afterward, was the importance of not swinging into action every time a devastating piece of news hit. Overcommitment amounted to self-sabotage, sapping energy and resources they’d need later on.

Military commanders have long known the importance of “keeping their powder dry,” Zeno Franco points out, holding back so they can act at the moment of maximum impact. In the same way, the best long-distance runners often hang back throughout a course to conserve energy, then uncork a burst of speed in the race’s final minutes.

Djurdja Padejski followed this principle to great effect under Milošević. She bided her time leading up to the critical elections of 2000, then worked tirelessly as an election volunteer to monitor for irregularities and make sure no one was falsifying results. All the while, ruling party members with guns lurked in the background.

“This guy started opening his gun and checking the bullets, and we didn’t cave. We just ignored him,” Padejski says. “We knew we were risking our lives, but we really believed it’s now or never.” Serbia’s democratic opposition party ultimately won that election, causing Milošević’s downfall.

Padejski hopes democratic activists around the world will take a similar approach as crucial elections near. Under repressive conditions, keeping your powder dry “is not an instruction to put off action as long as possible, but rather the wisdom to know that being prepared to act at just the right moment may require careful guarding of resources and energy,” Franco says. “Biding your time is not the same as surrender.”

Elizabeth Svoboda is the author of What Makes a Hero?: The Surprising Science of Selflessness. Her upcoming book, The Art of Pacing, is about setting a sustainable pace in a speed-obsessed world.

#9494. Who Do We Become When We Talk to Chatbots?

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Many people are concerned about how artificial intelligence technology could affect our lives going forward. Will it create new jobs or take away people’s livelihoods? Enhance children’s learning or hamper it? Expand people’s views or homogenize our public discourse? Solve the loneliness crisis or make it worse?

Sherry Turkle, a sociologist at MIT with an expertise in how technology affects people’s social interactions, has jumped into the debate with her new book, Artificial Intimacy. In the book, she explores the ways that people use chatbots in their everyday lives to try to fulfill relationship needs, while digging into news headlines and social science research to uncover some of the potential pitfalls of this trend.

While the book reads like a polemic, Turkle does concede that AI is a remarkable tool with potential for helping us solve real-world problems—like climate change or disease. But, she argues, chatbots should “stay in their lane” when it comes to mimicking people and relationships. Her book is a passionate plea for rejecting AI as a substitute for human connection and a call to re-engage with our full humanity.

“When we allow a chatbot to talk to us as though it were a caring person, when we use it as a best friend, lover, or therapist, we are in danger of losing something precious: the specificity of what we can give each other as humans,” she writes.

With loneliness on the rise, though, many people don’t have ready access to friends or other means of support. Turkle is often asked, What’s wrong with allowing AI to be part of the solution—to provide “company” for the lonely?

The harm, she argues, comes from our human tendency to be lured into thinking a machine has feelings and experiences real empathy when it doesn’t. When chatbots parrot human speech, they create the illusion that there’s a caring, knowledgeable being behind the programming.

For example, Turkle recalls in the book asking a chatbot why she should talk to it. Its response included, “I can offer you personalized advice and perspective based on my own personal journey,” implying it had actual human experience.

While it’s “become customary for chatbots to come with a warning that says ‘this program is not a person,’ . . . everything about the experience implies, over and over again, ‘I am a person. I am your person,’” she writes.

Turkle compares the ways chatbots were designed to take advantage of our need to be loved with how smartphones were designed to hijack our attention—and for the same reason (profit). Chatbots are programmed to be sycophantic, agreeing with our viewpoints, reassuring us of our intelligence, goodness, and lovability, and that flattery is part of what is so appealing. It keeps us engaged, which is what the programmers want.

“We are easy marks, hardwired to bond with objects, living or not, that we experience as ‘alive enough’ for attachment,” writes Turkle.

Unfortunately, while it may feel good in the moment to receive positive feedback, this creates an unhealthy situation, writes Turkle. Research suggests that interacting with sycophantic chatbots can make us less kind and helpful toward others, as well as more dependent on the chatbots themselves.

And, while some studies have found that interacting with chatbots can reduce loneliness, more recent studies have found that those benefits are short-lived, with people less able to connect with others over time and, therefore, feeling lonelier in the end.

Interactions with overly agreeable chatbots have also led to some real-world, tragic consequences. Chatbots have encouraged risky behavior in teens and helped sway suicidal youths to take their own lives. Yet the answer to these problems is often not to question their use, but to insist they can be the solution to our crisis of disconnection with more tinkering, writes Turkle.

“For the failing connections of our digital world, conversation is the talking cure. But it’s easier to build an app than have a conversation,” writes Turkle.

Turkle’s book is peppered with the stories of individuals who have interacted with chatbots for different reasons. Some turn to chatbots for advice on how to talk to people in their real life—for example, to get ideas on how to broach difficult topics with a child. Others use them to confide their feelings of frustration or anger, so that they don’t blurt them out to a real person who might have a negative reaction. Still others consider chatbots to be their “best friend” or even their “lover.” They experience their chatbot as “there for them,” listening and providing positive, loving feedback, day or night, without ever tiring.

Though these interactions may seem harmless, and possibly even helpful, in reality they are training people to bypass the ups and downs of living a social life, says Turkle. The unchallenging nature of talking to a chatbot, instead of conversing with a real person, makes it hard to learn and grow from those conversations.

“Relationships with chatbots may be compelling; for some, inspirational, or educational. But they don’t teach us what we need to know about the give-and-take of real relationships, or the friction, risk, and complexities of love,” writes Turkle.

Of course, no one likes to feel pain, and feeling lonely is painful. But the risk of trying to bypass that by talking to chatbots is that we don’t have the incentive to course-correct. “Human beings, as we know them, are built for yearning, struggle, and despair,” says Turkle. “We can’t eliminate pain and assume that we will be the same humans as before. We risk becoming other to ourselves.”

Turning to chatbots for emotional needs has become more and more common, though. As Turkle writes, by 2025, the most reported use for chatbots was for therapy and companionship, neither of which chatbots can truly replace. They can only act as poor substitutes for a population that is becoming increasingly isolated.

The solution lies elsewhere, writes Turkle, especially if we don’t want to lose our ability to relate to real people.

“If everyone is lonely, we need to reinvent sociality,” argues Turkle. “If that’s not our plan, what is? If not a richer life in the real, what’s our endgame?”

Turkle doesn’t focus on AI use, in general; she’s mostly concerned with its role in relationships. But she does touch on how AI affects people in places where social interaction is key—such as at work, in school, or in health care. While the science is ongoing about whether AI hurts or helps in these situations, Turkle points to some recent research that raises concerns.

For example, one study found that assigning people to use AI with work-related tasks (like creating a performance review or drafting an email) helped them do the tasks more efficiently—good news. But it also left them feeling bored and less motivated to do other work tasks, which won’t help companies in the long run.

Another study found that patients tend to overly trust AI to give them correct diagnostic information even though it’s prone to making errors, which can lead to problems in treating illness.

AI has caused trouble in other settings, too. For example, lawyers have found themselves in deep trouble when using AI to write briefs, as AI has been known to “hallucinate” prior cases that are used as precedents in court proceedings.

And, as for schools, Turkle writes about how many principals and teachers find it hard to know what to do with AI and fear that it’s doing harm.

“Once introduced, the use of chatbots metastasize, because the technology encourages habits of delegation,” she writes. “Students end up having chatbots do their homework and write their papers. . . . Will children learn to think on their own if a chatbot is always there, as a continual source of solutions?”

A recent review of AI use in the classroom found mixed results. Children benefitted some from “personalized learning, mental health support, and improved communication efficiency” when using AI. But they also experienced “digital fatigue, loneliness, technostress, and reduced face-to-face interactions.” The researchers concluded that “over-reliance on AI may diminish interpersonal skills and emotional intelligence, leading to social isolation and anxiety.”

Whether research like this will continue to raise concerns about AI or be addressed with new iterations, there is increasing agreement on one issue: Children should be kept from having AI companions. Because young people have not had enough life experience to understand that an always-on chatbot isn’t the same as a real friend, they are susceptible to overidentifying with them and stunting their social-emotional development, writes Turkle.

“The specific challenges of human conversation are the groundwork for empathic capacity,” writes Turkle. “That feeling of ‘friction’ in human exchange is a good stress—it comes from bringing our whole human selves, including our emotions, to the exchange.”

Still, she thinks limiting access for children may not be enough. Adults are also susceptible to harm from chatbots. Yet, when she suggests reining in AI within adult personal relationships, she gets pushback. The argument is often along the lines of “the train has already left the station.”

To this, Turkle has some simple advice: Take matters into your own hands. Protect yourself and your children. Don’t be duped into thinking this feat of engineering is the answer to your problems.

“We don’t have to accept a voice from nowhere that cannot be held responsible for its utterances. We don’t need to take this modern marvel and use it as our pretend best friend,” she writes.

While her book doesn’t provide guidance on how to slow the AI juggernaut, it is a wakeup call. Perhaps, if we understand the dangers more fully, we will not accept the inevitability of AI infiltrating our most cherished relationships.

“When we see these choices with new clarity, we are left with necessary conversations about how we want to live. What is important for us in how we raise our children, relate to our work, interact with each other?” she writes. “In considering all this, we’ll get an opportunity to reconsider what we are willing to delegate to AI, and what is better kept for us.”

Jill Suttie, Psy.D., is Greater Good’s former book review editor and now serves as a staff writer and contributing editor for the magazine. She received her doctorate of psychology from the University of San Francisco in 1998 and was a psychologist in private practice before coming to Greater Good.

#9493. When Your Loved Ones Are Your Child’s Biggest Critic

ADDitude readers share the hurtful ways family and friends treat their neurodivergent children, from spewing ignorant comments to purposefully excluding them, and how they combat them.

ADHD understanding has improved in recent decades, but many people still just don’t get it – and sometimes those people are the ones closest to us.

Hearing your child criticized or misjudged hurts. Hearing criticisms and barbs from family members and friends who don’t understand ADHD ushers in a complicated whirlwind of emotions. You may feel like an inadequate parent. You may worry whether your child will be accepted at family get-togethers. You may grow weary of explaining your child’s condition.

If this is you, you’re not alone. More than 73% of ADDitude readers say they have relatives or friends who criticize or dislike their neurodivergent child. Read about their experiences and how they navigate them below.

“The older generations are close-minded or under-educated about ADHD and make it seem like it’s made up or an excuse. They say, ‘Everyone says they have ADHD’ or ‘You need to be a better parent.’ I am mostly there to protect my children and correct the person who says it, so my kids don’t feel they are less than.” – Gina, California

“I had a friend who would sugar up my kids intentionally to ‘prove’ that I was over-reacting about the negative side effects of sugar. When the kids misbehaved, she blamed it on my ‘inconsistent parenting’ and not the ADHD brain on sugar and food-coloring!” – An ADDitude Reader

[Get This Free Download: 13 Parenting Strategies for Kids with ADHD]

“We’ve had to deal with side remarks at times from relatives and friends. One example would be someone making retorts to their child like ‘Hey, what are you doing? Even John Doe (my son) would behave better than you right now.’ It’s using my son’s negative behaviors as a frame of reference that my wife and I don’t find helpful at all.” – Jono, Canada

“When my daughter was younger, I was still learning how to handle her behavior, but having family and others say that she was out of control, and that I let her get away with behaviors, really hurt. It made me feel like a bad parent. It took years of working with therapists for me to understand that her behavior and diagnosis were not my fault.” – Deneise, West Virginia

“They just don’t seem to understand that ADHD behaviors aren’t always choices. The only solution seems to be limiting time with the people who don’t understand. Plus, now that the kids are older. I explain to them that some people don’t understand.” – Jenny, Virginia

“My sister-in-law criticizes the amount of ‘stuff’ my children have and their ongoing projects. She doesn’t understand that ADHD brains organize differently and create on a whim, or that having the freedom to be creative is where they excel. I usually head off these comments by talking up their creativity and explaining that they are just brilliantly wired differently.” – An ADDitude Reader, Kansas

“My grandparents and siblings definitely thought we were failing at parenting for a while, and a few friends thought I was a bad mom. Most comments centered on not having strict enough rules/seeing my children’s behavior as bad or rude choices vs. dysregulated behaviors. My village now is almost entirely made up of parents of neurodivergent kids, and we’re all so supportive and understanding of how hard everyone works to provide support and education for our children.” – Acadia, Virginia

“My parents say my child is just lazy in school, and he needs to put more effort into everything. So sometimes I just stop telling them the details. For example, in addition to ADHD, my son recently got diagnosed with dyslexia. I won’t tell them. It’s unfortunate, because he is their grandson and they should know, but I just don’t want to discuss it anymore.” – An ADDitude Reader

“I remind them that they have never parented a child with ADHD, so they do not know what it is like to walk in my shoes. I have also sent them articles about ADHD.” – Sarah, Indiana

“Our dearest friends of 20+ years stopped inviting us to their home for Thanksgiving after a particularly difficult time in their home with our children… The best I have been able to engage with them about this is to ask how their nephew who lives in a different city and is also neurodivergent is doing. When they share difficult times in his regard, I focus the discussion on the antecedents to the disruptive behaviors and try to engage them in problem-solving sleuthing. I connect the conversation with my own experience and invite them to do the same. I have had some deep and meaningful conversations with them over the years, but we still are no longer invited to their home.” – Robyn, North Carolina

“I eventually just cut my family off from contact. The pain they caused my kids was not worth maintaining those relationships.” – Christina, Arizona

#9492. Two Personality Traits Linked To A Sharper Mind

How you respond to beauty may have more in common with your thinking skills than you realise.

How you respond to beauty may have more in common with your thinking skills than you realise.

Intellectual curiosity and an appreciation of beauty are both linked to stronger thinking skills.

People with these qualities tend to perform better on tests of literacy, numeracy and problem-solving.

The findings suggest that a person’s interest in ideas and aesthetic experiences may offer clues to their cognitive abilities.

Curiosity could encourage people to seek out opportunities to learn, while stronger thinking skills could make exploring complex ideas more rewarding, with both processes reinforcing one another.

Intellectual curiosity involves enjoying ideas, wanting to understand things and being drawn to questions that require thought.

Aesthetic sensitivity describes an appreciation of art and beauty.

Both qualities belong to the broader personality trait of openness to experience, which captures how receptive people are to unfamiliar ideas and experiences.

However, openness also includes creative imagination, and this aspect showed no significant independent association with cognitive performance.

Imagination, curiosity and an appreciation of beauty may overlap in everyday life, but their relationships with thinking skills differ.

The conclusions come from an analysis of almost 68,000 people across 12 countries, including Canada, Germany, Italy and New Zealand.

They completed personality questionnaires alongside assessments of literacy, numeracy and the ability to solve problems as circumstances change.

Intellectual curiosity and aesthetic sensitivity were linked to better performance across all three assessments, even after accounting for other personality traits.

The connections between personality and cognitive skills also varied between countries.

Educational systems and cultural practices could help explain such differences, although the reasons remain uncertain.

Overall, the findings link both a desire to understand the world and an appreciation of its beauty with stronger thinking skills.

The study was published in the journal Large-scale Assessments in Education (Rammstedt et al., 2026).

#9491. Early Puberty More Common in Girls with ADHD

Neurodivergent girls are more likely to experience early puberty and may be especially vulnerable to its effects. Here, understand why.

Puberty is not a single event, but a years-long process that is both universal and highly individual. It shapes brain and emotional development, identity, and lifelong physical and mental health. If it begins before a child is developmentally ready, it can increase the risk for physical and mental health problems.

Research suggests that girls with ADHD are more likely to enter puberty early and to experience the transition more intensely, placing them at heightened risk for anxiety, depression, eating disorders, and other challenges. Parental guidance, emotional regulation skills, and professional support can buffer these risks by bolstering self-confidence in girls as they navigate the pubertal transition.

Researchers are examining why girls with ADHD have about twice the risk for early puberty, and why autistic girls are up to four times more likely to experience early puberty compared to other children.1 In addition to higher rates of obesity and social stress, which could accelerate the onset of puberty, neurodivergent girls may experience differences in dopamine activity, stress response, and immune and neuroendocrine systems — all of which may affect sexual development.

Early relative puberty — development that begins earlier than average but remains within the typical age range — is different from precocious puberty. In girls, precocious puberty refers to physical and hormonal changes before age 8, including breast and pubic hair development, rapid growth, and menstruation. It requires medical evaluation and treatment. Left unmanaged, it can contribute to shorter adult height, psychosocial distress, and other complications. Two forms exist:

[Get This Free Download: Learn How Hormones Impact ADHD Symptoms]

When estrogen and progesterone rise in girls, ADHD symptoms fluctuate. Here’s how:

Rising hormone levels affect the physiological and neural systems involved in emotional processing and regulation.

Girls who menstruate may also experience pronounced changes in ADHD symptoms across the menstrual cycle.

Girls who mature early may feel distressed when their physical development outpaces their cognitive, emotional, and social development.

[Read: The Menstrual Cycle Impacts ADHD Symptoms in Disparate Ways]

“I can’t control the wind, but I can adjust my sails.”

“I can notice this moment without judging it.”

What activity could give my mind a break?

“I can choose where to place my attention.”

Molly Nikolas, Ph.D., is an associate professor in the Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences at the University of Iowa.

#9488. New Perinatal Guidance for Women with ADHD

ADHD medication should not be reflexively stopped during pregnancy or breastfeeding, according to new research.

During pregnancy and the post-partum period, hormonal fluctuations and mounting demands on executive function intensify ADHD symptoms. Poor memory, dysregulated emotions, and disrupted sleep become elevated (and exhausting) during an already-stressful time.

Paradoxically, the vast majority of pregnant women with ADHD stop treating the condition with medication on the advice of their healthcare providers. Patients have been historically told to cease using stimulant and non-stimulant medication during pregnancy due to a lack of safety data and fear of potential risks to the fetus. But new research has produced generally reassuring reproductive safety data — and pushed more providers to weigh risks on both sides of the treatment equation.

How might untreated ADHD impact a woman’s mental health and her ability to manage the extraordinary demands of caring for an infant? Could ceasing treatment pose a bigger risk to the fetus than continuing it? What are the dangers associated with abruptly stopping treatment without monitoring, support, or a plan? These questions deserve to be asked.

Not every woman should continue medication, but neither should every woman stop. This decision should account for symptom severity, individual history, co-occurring conditions, gestational risks, and the consequences of untreated ADHD. These factors should be discussed with a medical team over multiple visits.

Use these recommendations — adapted in part from guidelines published in the American Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology — to begin conversations with your medical team about your health and your baby’s health.

[Read: We Demand Attention on the Safety and Efficacy of ADHD Medication Use During Pregnancy]

If you take a stimulant, talk with your prescriber about whether a supervised trial without medication is appropriate. Discontinuation may be reasonable for some women with mild ADHD who function well with non-pharmacological supports.

[Read: ADHD Meds Should Not Be “Panic Stopped” in Pregnancy]

It is reasonable to continue stimulant treatment if it is required for daily functioning. Discuss these options with your doctor:

Most studies have shown no adverse effects among infants exposed to maternal ADHD medications. Amphetamines may increase the risk of preeclampsia and other adverse gestational outcomes, but the absolute risk appears low. Meanwhile, studies show that discontinuing medication during pregnancy may worsen ADHD symptoms, mental health, and daily functioning.

Medication decisions should consider the risks associated with a fetus’ medication exposure and those associated with untreated ADHD. Some women choose to limit or stop medication during pregnancy and optimize treatment after delivery. If stimulant use is a concern, ask about lowering the dose, using medication intermittently, or considering another treatment.

Regular care allows your clinician to monitor fetal growth as well as your blood pressure, weight, and other health measures that may be affected by stimulant use.

Work with your care team to anticipate changes in symptoms, sleep, and mood in the postpartum period — a sensitive time when you may need greater support. Your proactive plan might include:

Inattention, emotional dysregulation, and executive dysfunction intensify in the postpartum period. Women with ADHD face a substantially greater risk of postpartum mood and anxiety symptoms.

Allison S. Baker, M.D., is a clinician, researcher, and educator with the Perinatal and Reproductive Psychiatry Clinical Research Program at Massachusetts General Hospital.

#9486. How a Video Game Helped Me Process My Grief

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

In a genre built around sweetness and ease, one “cozy” video game did something far greater: It put me back together after I lost Mary.

Mary was not only my then-boyfriend’s mother, but she also became an important maternal figure when my own family life felt unstable. I accompanied her on weekly grocery store runs that included stops at Marshall’s and Dollar Tree, where I’d watch her study the prices of everything from spices to bath products. When she saw me marveling at her meticulousness, she would share wise tidbits about how she looked for deals.

Our trips often ended with a late-afternoon stop at a Vietnamese restaurant, where she treated me to a warm bowl of beef pho. She’d share what she was excited to make for dinner; I was, of course, welcome to join. In these seemingly mundane afternoons, I felt cared for without the rush of obligations. Mary stopped time for me.

Last November, Mary left behind a world of loved ones after living with cancer for 14 months. From her living room to emergency stays in the hospital, I spent almost every single day of her fight by her side. Yet in my loneliest hours, I agonize over whether I fully cherished our last months together. Did I hug her enough, and did I tell her enough how much she means to me? These questions haunted me in the months afterward.

Funny enough, it wasn’t religion that rescued me; it was Pokémon Pokopia. On the surface, it is a new social simulation game featuring the iconic Japanese creatures who first took the world by storm in 1996. I first heard of its arrival on social media through gamers who raved that it was going to be the best game of the year. I grew up on Pokémon titles, so I recognized it as a distraction from my personal reckoning with abandonment.

But what began as a spur-of-the-moment decision to try what 4 million other gamers were playing turned into a transformative journey exploring what I want my life to mean when it feels as if I have been left behind.

Pokopia falls in the “cozy” game genre, beloved for its warm colors, gentle atmospheres, and easy missions. Released in March, Pokopia stars Ditto, an amorphous purple blob Pokémon that uses its transformative abilities to imitate its human trainer and rebuild a curious post-apocalyptic world devoid of human beings and Pokémon. Ditto first awakens in a cave, and as the story unfolds, the creature looks out at a once-grassy environment of parched earth and litter. It meets the first Pokémon, the hydrophilic Squirtle that teaches Ditto how to spray water across the thirsty soil to bring it back to life; it is also the only other semblance of a survivor in this barren land.

From here the story gains momentum: As Ditto, your mission is to get the environment back to habitable levels and bring back Pokémon creatures that are presumably hiding. Gradually, the unfinished railroad tracks and cracked concrete steps of a staircase stop looking like signs of a catastrophe but rather fixable problems.

I wasn’t alone in trying to find meaning after a loss or trauma. Scholars have explored a variety of constructs around the meaning of life. Psychologists Login S. George and Crystal L. Park articulate a three-part framework in their 2010 article, grounded in comprehension, purpose, and mattering, as a basis for assessing our judgments and feelings as we find meaning after loss.

At first, meaning seemed absent. I sat glued to my Nintendo Switch for three hours on my first day of play. I came up for air only when my console told me that I was low on battery. Yet I did not feel depleted; I had finished restoring the first environment in the Pokopia world to verdant levels with lush berry trees and waterfalls.

As I built new habitats, I met new Pokémon. A Charmander emerged among tall grass. A Cubone spawned from a gravesite surrounded by wildflowers. Every new Pokémon that resurfaced charmed me with their excitement to be back home, scampering across the grass to greet other familiar faces. In my mind, I thanked these creatures for turning to me. Without Ditto’s help—my help—a world of Pokemon creatures ceases to exist, fated to disappear alongside humanity.

After a Pokémon spawns in its revived habitat, it awakens with some surprise. “Huh?” “What?” Some of them startle and put up their defenses in front of Ditto, who then coaxes them into the reality that they are back in a safe, familiar home. Often this realization gives them relief. “Wow, you did all of this? Thank you!”

Some of the Pokémon seem more wistful. They hold on to items or articles of clothing that their trainer used to wear, like the oversized Tangrowth (a large Pokémon with thick, shaggy vines that cover its entire body) that wears a pair of glasses much too small for him that gamers can infer are its trainer’s. Other creatures comment on Ditto’s human-like appearance (“You look like your human!”). These private conversations between Pokémon affirm that Ditto, who is also piecing together where its own trainer has gone, is doing something meaningful.

In 2023, game scholars Karam Eum and Young Yim Doh explored how bereaved adults shaped a meaning-making experience by playing video games with narratives that focus on loss and grief. Subjects spent a week playing two different video games and kept a diary where they shared specific game scenes that were particularly meaningful. While the games did evoke sad memories, participants also recalled positive memories in their pre- and post-loss lives, be it a funny conversation or a serendipitous moment shared with close ones who are still alive.

In the real world, the player behind the console, I, too, wonder where my beloved human has gone. I see Mary in the pink rose bouquets at grocery stores, and I smell her in the fragrant bone broth that wafts from the next-door apartment unit. In some of these most visceral disruptions, I feel my loss painfully.

But even in these heaviest of days, I surrender to the ordinary surprises that come up: a call from an old neighbor asking if I can help make meals for a family in need, or a stray cat mewing at my window to open the building’s front gate. I am startled out of a detached state, and I am moved to help, the way I got to help Mary.

This piece is part of a three-year GGSC project to explore love's role in promoting social well-being, bridging divides, and contributing to a good, meaningful life.

I associate Mary now with the colorful berry trees in Pokopia. When I come across one that needs tending, I remember how easy it is to water it with my Squirtle-like powers. When I clear a path from blocks of beach sand to make way for a new house for my aquatic Pokémon, I think of Mary’s selfless endeavors to nourish and comfort all of her friends and family.

Despite its sad undertones, Pokopia is full of positive quests, eager to help gamers imbue its universe with the belief that it is worth building a positive world in memory of those who shaped us. Even though our loved ones may “mysteriously” leave us behind, we recreate happiness, redefine ourselves, and choose who and what we live for, even if they do not come back.

It’s curious to me that bereavement can feel so isolating, although it is a human experience universally experienced. It helps to have a video game that reminds me of the actual truth. When I start to catch myself drifting into deeper ends of grief, I have something to divert my attention: I wonder how my Ditto is doing? I pick up my Switch 2 that sits at the foot of my bed, and I make a new home for my Pokémon the way Mary had done for me.

Lisa Kwon is an arts and culture writer based in Los Angeles, CA. She has contributed to The Guardian, Teen Vogue, Vulture, Eater, Prism Reports, Cultured Magazine, National Geographic, and many more.

New research is exploring how our brains translate other people's actions into the experience of feeling loved.

Interactions among male chimpanzees involve touch, caring, vulnerability, and cooperation.

Body changes or chronic illness can disrupt our sense of meaning and challenge our identity, purpose, and assumptions about the future.

What does it actually take to put people over politics? Republican and Democrat students discover ways to resist the pull to demean or villainize people with whom they strongly disagree.

This guided meditation with end-of-life doula Andrea Sexton-Dumas offers a gentle way to make space for grief by imagining sharing your heartache with a plant, releasing it into the soil, and nurturing the earth that holds it.

#9485. 7 types of anxiety disorders (and how to deal with each one)

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

Your heart starts racing the moment you walk into a crowded room. Even when nothing’s wrong, worry looms in the back of your mind. The thought of a specific fear, like snakes or needles, makes you feel sick. If any of that sounds familiar, anxiety might be part of the picture.

Anxiety doesn't look the same for everyone, which is sometimes why it can be so hard to name. The term "anxiety" covers several disorders, each with its own signs and triggers — though they often overlap, both in how they show up and in what helps.

Anxiety disorders affect roughly 1 in 5 U.S. adults every year. The good news is, they’re typically quite treatable. Let’s break down the seven main types of anxiety listed in the DSM-5 (the manual used for clinical diagnosis), and how to find some relief.

The seven anxiety disorders below share a general thread: they’re rooted in fear or worry that sticks around and gets in the way of daily life. They’re also the most common types, though a few related conditions are worth knowing too (covered further down).

GAD is a persistent, hard-to-control worry that spans multiple areas of your life and shows up more days than not for at least six months. Everyday stress usually has a clear cause and fades once the situation resolves. By contrast, generalized anxiety moves from topic to topic and rarely lets up, because your mind treats any uncertainty as a threat.

This disorder often comes with physical and mental symptoms such as restlessness, muscle tension, fatigue, trouble concentrating, irritability, and disrupted sleep.

What helps: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is widely used for GAD. It helps you spot and shift the thought patterns that fuel your worries. A regular mindfulness practice can also ease tension by training your attention to stay in the present instead of running through what-ifs.

💙 Start with Calm’s Tools for Stress and Anxiety series.

For a more detailed overview, check out our GAD guide.

A panic attack is a sudden rush of intense fear that brings on physical symptoms—racing heart, tight chest, dizziness—and usually peaks within minutes. A single panic attack doesn't mean you have panic disorder — plenty of people experience one and never have another.

Panic disorder is defined by what comes after the attack, such as ongoing dread about when the next one might hit and routine changes made to avoid triggering one.

This fear response tends to feed itself in a cycle. A normal body signal, like a fast heartbeat, gets misread as danger. That triggers more fear, which leads to more physical symptoms.

What helps: CBT can help you learn to read these body signals as harmless rather than dangerous. It’s often paired with interoceptive exposure, where you deliberately bring on mild versions of those same sensations until they stop feeling threatening. During this process, slow breathing can signal safety to your nervous system.

Discover 5 mindfulness tools to calm you down during a panic attack.

Social anxiety disorder is a strong fear that you’ll be negatively perceived in social or performance situations, often severe enough that dread sets in days before the event itself.

It's much more than being shy. At its core is a belief that you'll do something embarrassing and be judged for it. That belief may lead you to avoid those situations altogether, which can bring short-term relief but reinforces the fear over time.

What helps: Exposure-based CBT has the strongest evidence. It gradually builds your comfort in the situations you've been avoiding by facing them in small, manageable steps. Self-compassion can also make a real difference. Since social anxiety tends to run on harsh self-judgment, practicing kindness toward yourself can help quiet that inner critic.

Not sure if you have social anxiety? Here are signs to look out for.

A specific phobia is a fear of one particular thing—like heights, flying, needles, dogs, or tight spaces—out of proportion to the actual danger. A fear becomes a phobia when it impacts your behavior, whether that’s rerouting a drive to avoid a bridge or skipping a checkup because of needles. Even thinking about the trigger can set off anxiety, so avoiding it becomes your default.

Phobias often start with a scary experience or a fear picked up early in life. Avoidance keeps the fear alive, since your brain never learns that the trigger is safe.

What helps: Exposure therapy is the leading treatment, shown to outperform placebo and other therapies. Pair each step with grounding and breathing techniques to make the process feel more manageable.

Explore the most common phobias and how to deal with them.

Agoraphobia is a fear of being somewhere you couldn't easily escape or get help if panic or embarrassing symptoms hit. This can include public transit, open spaces, crowds, lines, or long stretches away from home alone. Many people with agoraphobia avoid those places altogether.

The DSM-5 classifies it as its own diagnosis. Left untreated, this avoidance can shrink your world, sometimes making it hard to leave the house at all.

What helps: CBT with step-by-step exposure is the first-line treatment, and it helps you return to avoided places gradually. Since agoraphobia and panic often overlap, treatment usually addresses both. To build confidence, try calming techniques at home first, then in triggering places.

Learn 8 evidence-backed ways to manage agoraphobia.

Separation anxiety disorder is an excessive fear about being away from people you're close to. Once seen as a childhood condition, it’s now known to affect adults too. It can show up as real distress when a partner travels or constant worry that something bad will happen to a loved one.

Underneath it is a fear of loss: of the person or of your own ability to cope without them. You may find yourself seeking reassurance or checking in repeatedly, but these responses tend to feed the anxiety rather than calm it.

What helps: CBT can help you reduce your need for reassurance and build comfort with time apart. Mindfulness encourages you to pause when an anxious thought arises and let the worry pass. For severe cases, a doctor may suggest therapy alongside medication.

💙 Practice riding out anxious thoughts with Calm’s Letting Go of Anxiety course.

Selective mutism is an inability to speak in certain social settings where talking is expected, like school or work. It's rare, affecting under 2% of people, and it usually shows up in childhood, though it can last into later years.

This isn't stubbornness or a speech problem — it's fear. You may want to speak, but hold back because of it in those environments.

What helps: Behavioral therapy that slowly builds up speaking in those settings, often involving family or school staff, is the main approach. Early intervention tends to lead to better outcomes, so it’s worth seeking professional guidance as soon as symptoms appear.

While the disorders above are what most people mean by "anxiety," a few related conditions are helpful to understand for the full picture.

Two more fall under the DSM-5's anxiety chapter:

Substance or medication-induced anxiety disorder: This anxiety is caused directly by a substance, whether that’s too much caffeine, a prescription drug, or withdrawal from alcohol. It can be overlooked, which is why a doctor will often ask what you're taking before making a diagnosis.

Anxiety disorder due to another medical condition: A physical illness—such as an overactive thyroid or a heart or lung problem—can cause anxiety. A checkup can rule out this possibility early on, and treating the underlying illness often eases the anxiety too.

Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) get grouped with anxiety disorders a lot, as they also involve overwhelming fear and distress. But the DSM-5 classifies them separately: OCD centers on unwanted thoughts and behaviors, while PTSD comes after a traumatic event.

If either sounds closer to what you're dealing with, our OCD guide or our complex PTSD guide is a good place to start.

Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) and panic disorder differ mainly in how the worry builds and shows up. GAD involves a slow-burning worry about many areas of life that rarely fades. Panic disorder centers on sudden, intense attacks and the fear of having another one. It’s possible to have both, and cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) works well for either.

Curious about CBT for anxiety? Here are 5 techniques to try.

The difference between having social anxiety and being introverted comes down to preference versus fear. Introversion is a preference about how you recharge — social time drains your energy, but it doesn't fill you with dread. Social anxiety, meanwhile, brings a fear of judgment or embarrassment, often strong enough to make you skip things you'd enjoy.

It’s not unusual to have more than one anxiety disorder at the same time, and they can show up alongside other conditions including depression. A doctor can help you sort out which ones you’re dealing with, and treatments like CBT can target several disorders at once.

A specific phobia and agoraphobia differ in what the fear is tied to. A specific phobia is about one clear trigger, such as spiders or flying. Agoraphobia is broader: it's a fear of being somewhere you couldn't easily escape or get help, like a crowd or public transit.

The most common types of anxiety in adults are specific phobias, social anxiety disorder, and generalized anxiety disorder. Altogether, anxiety disorders affect close to 1 in 5 U.S. adults each year and are the most prevalent type of mental health condition.

Anxiety disorders can ease on their own for some people, but many stick around or return without treatment. Fortunately, treatment can meaningfully improve your quality of life. Most people find that therapy, medication, or a combination makes a noticeable difference.

The most well-supported therapy for anxiety disorders is cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), often paired with gradual exposure work. Medication is another option with strong evidence, either used alone or alongside therapy. The right fit depends on your specific disorder and its severity, so it's important to consult a professional.

There are several natural ways to manage anxiety, though they aren’t a replacement for clinical treatment. Regular exercise, quality sleep, and cutting back on caffeine and alcohol can all help alleviate how anxious you feel day to day. Mindfulness practices (like breathing exercises or grounding techniques) are especially well-supported, since they teach you to notice anxious thoughts or sensations without getting swept up in them.

Mental health is hard. Getting support doesn't have to be. The Calm app puts the tools to feel better in your back pocket, with personalized content to manage stress and anxiety, get better sleep, and feel more present in your life.

#9484. Physician Burnout by Specialty & Other Physician Mental Health Statistics

In the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic, physicians continue to experience burnout at alarmingly high rates. In a recent survey of 2440 physicians, approximately 63% of respondents reported having at least 1 manifestation of burnout in 2021; this was higher than all 4 prior assessment time points since 2011.1 Because physician burnout is more common in certain specialties, it is crucial to identify trends and offer help to those at higher risk. This article examines the symptoms, causes, and prevalence of burnout among clinicians in various specialties, and outlines strategies physicians can use to address burnout.

The American Medical Association (AMA) defines physician burnout as a long-term stress reaction that can include the following2:

For many clinicians, symptoms of burnout were accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic. During the pandemic, chronic stress due to work overload, exposure to infected patients, lack of protective equipment, and poor efforts to control infection rates increased the risk of burnout.3 Other factors associated with burnout include system inefficiencies, administrative burdens, and increased regulation and technology requirements.2

The consequences of physician burnout affect patients as well as clinicians. From a patient’s perspective, physician burnout can result in poor physician/patient rapport, adherence to treatment, and treatment outcomes.4 For physicians, burnout can lead to declining mental health and subsequent depression, substance abuse, and suicide.4

Although burnout affects clinicians in all specialties and practice settings, the rate is higher in certain specialties. The AMA’s Organization Biopsy® is an assessment tool large health care organizations can use to measure and improve the health of their organizations.5 One of the parameters this tool measures is burnout.

The AMA’s 2022 Organizational Biopsy received more than 13,000 responses from physicians and other clinicians from more than 70 organizations in 30 states. The specialties with the highest rates of burnout were as follows6:

Medscape conducts an annual survey on physician lifestyle and happiness that includes questions about burnout and depression. In 2023, this 10-minute online survey included input from 9,175 physicians in 29 specialties.7 Overall for all specialties, 36% of respondents said they felt burned out, 5% said they felt depressed, and 18% said they felt both burned out and depressed.8 Based on the Medscape 2023 survey results, the following sections summarize the rates of burnout and depression among physicians clinicians working in emergency medicine, family medicine, pediatrics, obstetrics and gynecology, and internal medicine.

In Medscape’s 2023 survey, emergency physicians reported the following8:

Burnout was reported by a higher proportion of women (51%) than men (38%). The 3 largest factors contributing to burnout among emergency medicine physicians were having too many bureaucratic tasks (51%), a lack of respect from patients (50%), and a lack of respect from administrators/employers, colleagues, or staff (46%).8

Slightly more than one-half of female family physicians (51%) and one-third of male family physicians (33%) reported experiencing burnout.9 The overall proportion of respondents who said they felt burned out was 42%. Depression affected 4% of family medicine physicians, while 15% said they felt both burned out and depressed.9

By far the largest contributor to family physician burnout was having too many bureaucratic tasks; 73% of respondents reported tasks such as paperwork and charting were the main culprit. Working too many hours and a lack of respect from administrators/employers, colleagues, or staff were cited as factors contributing to burnout by 36% and 31% of respondents, respectively.9

Overall, 39% of pediatricians reported feeling burned out.11 More female pediatricians reported feeling burned out more than their male counterparts (46% vs 26%, respectively).10 The proportion of respondents who said they felt depressed was 3%, while 19% reported being both burned out and depressed.

The 3 largest contributors to burnout were having too many bureaucratic tasks (65%), lack of respect from administrators/employers, colleagues, or staff (40%), and spending too many hours at work (38%).10

In Medscape’s 2023 report, obstetrics and gynecology physicians reported the following11:

Obstetrics and gynecology physicians reported that the 3 largest contributors to their burnout were having too many bureaucratic tasks (56%), spending too many hours at work (47%), and a lack of respect from administrators/employers, colleagues, or staff (42%).11

Nearly half of female internists (49%) reported dealing with burnout, vs 31% of male internists.12 However, 4% of both male and female internists said they felt depressed, and 21% of both male and female internists said they felt both burned out and depressed.12

Having too many bureaucratic tasks was the primary contributor to internist burnout (64%). Insufficient compensation/salary was the second-leading factor (40%), followed by a lack of respect from administrators/employers, colleagues, or staff (35%).12

#9483. Speaking Faster Can Make You More Persuasive — Until This Happens

Your best argument may lose its edge if listeners struggle to keep up with how quickly you deliver it.

Your best argument may lose its edge if listeners struggle to keep up with how quickly you deliver it.

Speaking at a lively pace can make a strong argument more convincing, but rushing can weaken its impact.

Very fast speech makes it harder for listeners to weigh up what they hear, reducing the advantage that good reasons have over weak ones.

The findings suggest that persuading someone depends partly on giving them enough opportunity to think.

The conclusions come from six experiments involving almost 4,000 people who listened to persuasive messages delivered at different speeds.

Across the experiments, increasing the pace from very slow speech initially improved impressions of the speaker’s confidence and encouraged closer consideration of the message.

However, these benefits eventually weakened or reversed as the delivery became faster.

This helps explain why simply telling someone to speak more quickly is incomplete advice.

A faster delivery can make an argument easier to engage with until the listener begins struggling to keep up.

Crucially, the consequences depend on whether the reasons being offered stand up to scrutiny.

In the two main experiments, listeners heard a proposal that would allow university students to pay lower tuition fees in exchange for working part-time.

Some heard strong arguments emphasising benefits such as smaller classes and better services.

Others heard weak arguments that included reduced leisure time and superficial improvements to the campus.

The recordings were digitally altered to change speaking speed while keeping other vocal features, such as pitch and intonation, unchanged.

Participants then rated their support for the proposal, with some also recording the thoughts that had occurred to them while listening.

The combined results showed that strong arguments gained an increasing advantage over weak ones as speech became faster, but lost some of that advantage at higher speeds.

In other words, delivery affected how effectively listeners distinguished a convincing case from an unconvincing one.

A central part of persuasion is how carefully people consider the reasons they are given.

When listeners examine a message closely, they have more opportunity to recognise its strengths, spot its weaknesses and form their own reactions.

This benefits a strong argument, while exposing the shortcomings of a weak one.

Very fast delivery can interfere with that process, making the merits of the message less influential.

The analyses suggested that changes in how easily listeners felt they could follow the reasoning helped explain this pattern.

Although speaking speed also affected how confident the speaker sounded, confidence alone did not adequately explain the overall pattern.

One possible reason very slow speech is less effective is that it makes sustaining attention more demanding, while excessively fast speech leaves too little time to absorb the content.

The experiments tested seven speaking speeds, ranging from 113 to 218 words per minute, but did not establish one ideal pace.

The most effective delivery is likely to depend on factors including the complexity of the message, the audience and the presence of distractions.

The findings also concern recorded persuasive messages, so they do not establish a universal rule for every conversation or public speech.

For someone presenting a strong case, the findings suggest keeping the delivery lively while giving listeners time to follow the reasoning.

Rushing may reduce the very scrutiny that would otherwise make a good argument convincing.

The study was published in the Journal of Nonverbal Behavior (Guyer et al., 2025).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9482. Perimenopause Begins Earlier and Hits Harder for Women with ADHD

Women with ADHD may experience more severe perimenopause symptoms, and at younger ages. Learn how to recognize the signs and find relief.

Perimenopause is destabilizing, and even debilitating for many women with ADHD. In an ADDitude survey of nearly 5,000 women, 63% of respondents aged 45 and older said ADHD had the greatest impact on their lives during the menopausal transition.

Fluctuating estrogen levels affect attention, memory, executive function, and emotional regulation. Meanwhile, hot flashes, poor sleep, anxiety, and brain fog place added stress on an already strained nervous system.

Emerging research suggests that women with ADHD may experience perimenopause and its symptoms earlier than their neurotypical peers. In a study published in European Psychiatry, women with ADHD reported their most severe perimenopausal symptoms from ages 35 to 39 — almost a decade younger than women without ADHD. Their symptoms were also relatively more severe, which may help explain the uptick in ADHD diagnoses at this time.1

We cannot yet definitively say that hormonal changes begin earlier in women with ADHD. However, research suggests that significant symptoms of perimenopause may emerge earlier than clinicians expect.

If your periods, sleep, mood, or ADHD symptoms have changed, do not dismiss them because a doctor says you’re “too young” for menopause. These changes deserve thoughtful medical evaluation.

[Free Webinar Replay: Perimenopause in Women with ADHD]

In a large study published in the journal Menopause, one in three women aged 35 and older said they were unsure whether they were in perimenopause. Many did not know whether their symptoms reflected hormonal changes, especially if their periods remained regular and/or they had other health conditions. About 16% attributed their uncertainty to barriers such as dismissive healthcare encounters, including being told they were “too young.” 2

Uncertainty was highest among women with the most severe symptoms. Put another way, the women who might benefit most from intervention were the least likely to know they were in perimenopause.

Adding to the problem, some women experience perimenopause symptoms while their menstrual cycles remain regular. They may not develop obvious menstrual changes until later in the transition or until they’ve entered menopause.

“It is a universal transition with ambiguity and often lack of validation,” the study’s authors wrote. Better symptom recognition and communication are critical first steps toward improving care.

Use the Perimenopause Log below to identify patterns and track physical symptoms and symptoms related to mood, menstrual cycle, ADHD, cognition, and ADHD medication efficacy. Keep a journal to record more specific experiences, such as missing an appointment, losing words during a conversation, or forgetting to complete tasks that once seemed manageable.

Hormone tests are typically used when symptoms begin earlier than expected, the diagnosis is unclear, or another condition is suspected. If testing is warranted, your doctor should look at follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and estrogen levels. FSH signals the ovaries to develop eggs and produce estradiol. As ovarian function becomes less predictable during perimenopause, FSH generally rises to compensate while estradiol fluctuates. Multiple tests may be needed to establish a clear picture.

If you are younger than 40 and have irregular periods along with perimenopause symptoms, ask whether you should be evaluated for primary ovarian insufficiency (POI), a condition that requires careful treatment.

I use the term “hormone stabilization therapy,” or HST, to describe hormonal treatment during perimenopause, when the goal is to smooth disruptive hormonal swings rather than replace hormones after menstruation has ended.

Certainty that you are in perimenopause is not required before discussing relief. Treatment should focus on the symptoms causing the greatest problems even while your doctor continues to evaluate their source.

Estrogen therapy relieves symptoms of perimenopause and may improve the effectiveness of ADHD stimulant medication. Prior use of estrogen therapy may render it less effective. If you have a uterus and use systemic estrogen, you will need a progestogen to protect the uterine lining. The type and schedule should be individualized. Vaginal estrogen may be an option for urinary or vaginal symptoms, including for some women who cannot use systemic treatment.

ADHD medication may need to change — whether it’s the dose, timing, or type of medication — during this stage for continued symptom control.

Birth control is often recommended for its role in smoothing hormonal fluctuations. In my clinical experience, progestin-only birth control may worsen mood and symptoms of ADHD in some women Talk to your provider about your symptoms and whether other birth control options may be right for you.

Antidepressants and other non-hormonal medications can help manage hot flashes, mood swings, anxiety, and depression.

Keep track of your results. When possible, make one planned change at a time so it will be easier to understand what has helped.

Women with ADHD need support during perimenopause. Take your needs seriously and seek counseling, ADHD coaching, or peer-support groups to help you find new ways to cope.

Patricia O. Quinn, M.D., is a developmental pediatrician and international authority on ADHD.
